utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: The question, the important question that I need to address the Court on is the standard of review when evidence is admitted before the Appeal Chamber under Rule 115. It's important, we submit, to reflect, that no criminal justice system can be perfect, and as long as judges and jurors are human, human error will inevitably result in the innocent being convicted of crimes that they have not committed. The various domestic criminal jurisdictions of the world have developed rules of procedure and evidence that seek to minimise the chances of a wrongful conviction, and it's that jurisprudence that has been uplifted into the scheme of international law as reflected in the Rules and Procedure of this Tribunal. Every criminal justice system is fallible, and this Tribunal is no exception. The courts of England, the United States of America, and France are but three examples of countries where there have been celebrated cases where the innocent have been wrongly convicted and the protection afforded to an accused by the burden and standard of proof and the exclusionary rules of evidence have proved no safeguard. Inevitably, most criminal justice systems get it right most of the time. That involves necessarily many guilty people being acquitted. That is the price that every criminal justice system pays in order to minimise the risk of injustice to the innocent. The Statute of this Tribunal, in Article 25, provides in subparagraph (B) the power to reverse a decision of the Trial Chamber where, and I quote, "an error of fact has occasioned a miscarriage of justice." There is no definition of the words "miscarriage of justice." Perhaps no exhaustive definition is desirable. It is easy to say that a wrongful conviction of an innocent man is a miscarriage of justice. No one would complain about the inclusion of such an example within the parameters of those words. But the term "miscarriage of justice" is much wider than that. Examples: The conviction of a guilty man on perjured evidence can be but another example of a miscarriage of justice. When the Appeal Chamber admits evidence under Rule 115, it must do so, we submit, against the background of the burden and standard of proof and rules of exclusionary evidence that exist at trial. And when considering whether there has been a miscarriage of justice, if I could perhaps be forgiven by quoting from a common law jurist who, in giving the judgement of a court, in fact, in the court of appeal in England, said, and I just adapt the end to fit the facts of this case, when the appellant court said: "This court is not concerned with guilt or innocence of the appellants but only with the safety of their convictions. This may, at first sight, appear an unsatisfactory state of affairs until it is remembered that the integrity of the criminal process is the most important consideration for courts which have to hear appeals against conviction. Both the innocent and the guilty are entitled to fair trials. If the trial process is not fair, if it is distorted by deceit or by material breaches of the rules of evidence or procedure, then the liberties of all are threatened. This court is a court of review. The court reviews the trial process to equip itself to answer the question ..." And then adapting the words to fit those of the Tribunal: "Do we think there has been a miscarriage of justice? The court is not a court of trial or retrial." In New Zealand, in a case that's contained in my currently absent book of authorities, Mr. Justice Gault, in the case of the Queen and Dougherty, described a miscarriage of justice in a way that is consistent with the submissions advanced by the appellants in this appeal. He said: "The matter now to be determined is whether the evidence now available establishes that there was a miscarriage of justice." Those, of course, are the words of Article 25. "The appropriate approach," he says, "is to consider whether, had the evidence been available at trial, its cogency is such that it might reasonably have led the jury to a different verdict." And it's against that background that I invite this Appeal Chamber to consider the appropriate standard of review, where evidence has been admitted under Rule 115. First, as this Chamber is well aware, the appellant would have already satisfied the onerous test set before additional evidence is admitted, first annunciated by the Appeal Chamber in the case of Tadic and followed in a number of cases since. It's no part of my submission today to seek to criticise or go behind that high test. But it does mean that when evidence has been admitted by the Appeals Chamber, that high test of admissibility will have been crossed. And having satisfied that test, it is our submission that when applying the appropriate standard to the evidence that the Chamber has admitted, then justice can only be done if the Appeal Chamber asks itself the question posed in paragraph 232 of the appellant's brief; namely, "Might this evidence or could this evidence have resulted in the Trial Chamber arriving at a different verdict?" All acknowledge that there will be cases that can be easily disposed of when fresh evidence has been admitted. Few in number, but there will be or may be cases where the additional evidence demonstrates beyond doubt that the convicted person is innocent. It is easy to reflect upon what such evidence could be; perhaps the discovery of crucial DNA evidence which was not available hitherto that demonstrates he could not have been the person alleged to have been at the crime scene. There are obviously other examples that can be imagined. In such a case, the parties agree that this Court could comfortably conclude that there had been a miscarriage of justice and that no reasonable tribunal could convict, in which case the appropriate course of action would be to quash the conviction and direct a verdict of not guilty. There could be other cases at the other end of the spectrum where the weighted impact of the additional evidence when seen against the factual matrix at trial is such that no reasonable tribunal could have been influenced by the additional evidence, in which case all concede that the Appeal Chamber, despite having admitted the evidence, can nonetheless reject the appeal against conviction and uphold the verdict of the Trial Chamber. There is, of course, in the middle a substantial body of cases where the evidence would have the capacity to materially influence a decision of the Trial Chamber. What is the test to be applied there? There are three possible tests that could be applied. One is the Appeal Chamber could ask itself the question: Does the additional evidence demonstrate beyond reasonable doubt that the Trial Chamber would have decided the case differently? In other words, putting the burden on the appellant to seek to demonstrate to the criminal standard that there would have been a difference. As I understand it, the respondent does not suggest so onerous a test in this case. The remaining two reflect the difference between the parties here. One could be described as putting the burden on the appellant to demonstrate on the balance of probabilities so that it is more likely than not that the evidence admitted would have had an impact on verdict. And the second, the one that is advanced by me on behalf of the appellants, is that the evidence might or could have caused a reasonable tribunal of fact, or in this case a reasonable trial chamber, to have come to a different verdict. The difference between the words "would" and "could" is, we submit, significant. Both are in the past tense of the words "will" and "can." One imposes, we submit, an unreasonably high burden on an accused; the other is reflective of the same standard of proof that is to be found at Trial Chamber. I have sought to illustrate this by way of a homely example in the course of my skeleton. It is easy to imagine a case where there might be four eyewitnesses, all saying that the defendant was the person who killed a particular victim. And in the absence of any other evidence, apart from that of the accused himself who claims he was elsewhere, one can easily imagine how any reasonable trial chamber would conclude that the case against the accused was proved, and return a verdict of guilty. Thereafter, if we imagine that another witness is discovered who, through no fault of anybody, had not been traced at trial, who had a far better view of the crime than any of the other four, who was perhaps the teacher at the local school who had taught all, and she said, "Well, it wasn't the defendant, it was his brother," who all agree looked very much like him, now, in such a simple case as that, the appellant would never be able to satisfy an Appeal Chamber that that evidence would have resulted in a different verdict. My example proceeds upon the basis that all witnesses are accepted as being honest and either the four are mistaken or the one is mistaken. But in that example, the appellant would be unable to discharge the high burden described by them in their brief as onerous as put forward by the Prosecutor and would inevitably lose his appeal against conviction. In our submission, that would result in a miscarriage of justice certainly as defined by Mr. Justice Gault in the case that I’ve quoted from in New Zealand and ought, we submit, in any fair reflection of any criminal jurisprudence, result in a miscarriage of justice. Because in the example I have given, it would be perfectly possible for a reasonable tribunal of fact to have said in the light of this additional evidence, "Well, that raises a reasonable doubt in our mind whereby no means the defendant is by no means guilty, but he might be not guilty, and we can't rule it out as sensible possibility. Therefore our verdict must be one of not guilty remaining loyal of the burden of standard of proof as exists in a criminal trial before the Trial Chamber." Hence, in my example, the appellant would be found not guilty if that evidence as available at trial, but he could not have a conviction overturned in the absence of that evidence by an Appeal Chamber if the same evidence were called, and that must be a route, we submit, to injustice, particularly if one reflects on the circumstances in which the evidence was not called at trial. One of the routes to admissibility before this Chamber is that due diligence would not have discovered the evidence at trial so the appellant cannot be at fault for the Trial Chamber being kept in ignorance of this important piece of evidence. Indeed, hypothetically, the absence of the witness could be due to the Prosecutor failing to disclose her existence to the Court or the Defence. Such disclosure, hypothetically, being dishonest as well as innocent. One only has to reflect upon that as a possibility in order, we submit, to demonstrate why the test that we seek to urge the Court to apply to fresh evidence, when it is admitted, must be the right test and the fair test. It proceeds upon the basis as amplified by the Appeal Chamber in the course of the appeal of Tadic that reasonable people can come to different conclusions on the same facts. It is inherent in any system of justice that a tribunal of fact, that two different tribunals of fact hearing these same witnesses can reasonably come to a different conclusion. It is inevitable that conclusions in the criminal process will be dependent upon the view, an individual takes of a witness, the assessment of whether the witness is telling the truth or not, and views will inevitably vary, one judge from another. One is only to reflect not so much in this jurisdiction but in domestic jurisdictions where there are no juries how one can have dissenting judgements and do have dissenting judgements when guilt is being determined to demonstrate that even experienced judges can come to different views of the facts on the same evidence. Once one factors that into the assessment of additional evidence, it demonstrates, in our submission, how dangerous it is for the Appeal Chamber to slip into the task of acting as a court of review of the Trial Chamber's assessment of evidence, and even more dangerous for them to slip into the task of deciding what a Trial Chamber would do if they were to hear the additional evidence. On analysis, all that an Appeal Chamber can safely do, save in a clear case such as the two examples at either end of the spectrum about which there'd been no dispute; absent that, all the appeal Chamber can do is to say that a reasonable trier of fact or a reasonable trial chamber might or could have come to a different verdict had this evidence been placed before them. And we submit that that is the test that ought to be applied. To say "would" is to place an almost impossible burden on an appellant. First, the Appeal Chamber can't assess the witnesses. They don't hear the additional evidence. They don't hear the trial evidence. How on earth can the appeal Chamber, I ask rhetorically, actually assess whether the evidence would result in a different verdict without having seen or heard any of the witnesses? True, you may know what the conclusion of the Trial Chamber was who heard the uncontradicted evidence of a witness at trial, untested by the material disclosed by the route of the additional evidence here, but you do not know what the witness at trial would have said if confronted with the account disclosed in the additional evidence, nor how the witness would react to it when cross-examined; let alone what impact that would have on the Trial Chamber being able to sit, see, and observe the demeanour of the witness when so pressed; let alone can you say what the Trial Chamber's view would be of the additional evidence that even you have not heard from the witness themselves but have only seen in written form; let alone how that witness would perform in cross-examination. It is not beyond the bounds of the experience of all concerned in criminal justice that sometimes witnesses, when cross-examined, end up enhanced, so far as the Tribunal is concerned, rather than destroyed. Both can be the effect of robust cross-examination. And it is, we submit, a route to injustice to seek to resolve evidence without having it properly tested in an adversarial system. For one better or worse these tribunals operate under an adversarial system and it follows that important evidence must be tested under an adversarial system. So we submit that there are powerful reasons in logic why the lower threshold of "could" or "might" should be the standard adopted by the Appeal Chamber when considering evidence submitted under Rule 115. Such a test is entirely consistent with the Rules of the Tribunal. There is, of course, no clear guidance in Rule 115 as to what the -- where the burden lies and what the standard is for additional evidence. The Rules insofar as the impact on the Trial Chamber of course make it clear that, at that stage, the "would" or "might" test is applied effectively to a Trial Chamber when assessing evidence at first instance. We submit that there is no reason in logic why the same test ought not to be applied at the appellate stage, particularly where all agree that it was no fault of the appellant that the evidence was not called earlier. And being realistic, when one looks at the background of the circumstances in which these trials take place, inevitably, the collation of evidence is going to be a difficult task in many cases. Now, we submit that the test that we have advanced is one that is consistent with courts sitting in common law jurisdictions throughout the world. The civil law jurisdictions are, perhaps, not so readily comparable to the task that the Appeal Chamber is undertaking here. In many civil jurisdictions, following an ordinary criminal trial, there is a right to a fresh trial de novo. This does not, of course, exist in a common law jurisdiction and, therefore, one is considering a very different approach to a verdict from the -- that which you would have in, for example, France or Italy. Now, I accept, just as the previous decisions of the Appeal Chamber here, tend to use the words "would" or "could" interchangeably and as a consequence, really, neither side seeks to gain support from previous observations of the Trial Chamber because you can take your choice of a number of phrases that either support your submission or that of the respondent. So in domestic jurisdictions, it is right to say that there are many inconsistent uses of the words "would" and "could" in some countries, particularly United States of America. In England, the law is perfectly clear and there is no doubt at all that the position of the English common law is that the test advanced by the appellant here is the current state and, indeed, has been the state of the English common law for many years. It was most clearly set out in a celebrated decision of the House of Lords now many years ago where three of their lordships, Viscount Dilhouse, Lord Cross, and Lord Kilbrandon all set out in the clearest possible terms the test that is currently being advanced by the appellant today. Their quotations are set out on page 12 of the skeleton. I won't read them out again now. The Court will have them well in mind. That authority is today still regarded as the leading authority. It was followed in the celebrated case of the Queen and Clegg - no relation - in Northern Ireland, a celebrated case of the British soldier charged with the murder of a young girl when he was on patrol in Belfast. That same test applied by the Lord Chief Justice or Chief Justice Carswell there, and followed again in some of the more celebrated miscarriage of justice cases in England, all of the authorities of which are contained, in fact, in the first book of authorities that I know the Court has had for some time and is behind the earlier skeleton that I submitted. So it is only persuasive; of course, I acknowledge, in no sense binding on this Appeal Chamber. But there can be no doubt, and I think there was initially some doubt in the respondent's mind as to the effect of the English common law. I hope now there is no doubt. The English common law is clear. I have, in the missing book of authorities, identified a number of American authorities that are consistent with the test that I propose now. I conceded in the skeleton that there were other cases that would be consistent with the appellant's test and others that somehow seemed to fall in the middle. You can choose your state and choose your court and choose your test. It's perhaps a cynical way of looking at the authorities. I say this with great diffidence to the jurisdiction that I know the President comes from. But the fact remains that -- and I see today that there's a case in Massachusetts that clearly seems to support -- not Massachusetts, Maine, which was served today that supports the Prosecutor's test. And I acknowledge that there are others, in fact, that he has not, in fact, served but can be found in the encyclopaedia that I have copied that will also support his test, and there are others that support my test. What assistance the Court gets from such a conflicting view of authorities is a matter for the Court to reflect on. The, dare I say, more traditional common law jurisdictions, Canada, South Africa, Australia, New Zealand, we submit, all put their weight behind the "could" or "might" test in various ways. I have copied the two leading authorities from Canada in the book that's being copied as we speak now. Each of them speak of a test, and I just quote from the leading case of Palmer: "[The additional evidence] must be such that if believed it could reasonably, when taken with the other evidence adduced at trial, be expected to have affected the result." And quoting the approval from the earlier case of Martin, these are the crucial words: "It is enough," the additional evidence, "in my view, if the proposed evidence is of sufficient strength that it might reasonably affect the verdict of a jury." But I certainly don't propose any lower test. No one's suggesting that if it was unreasonable for the trier of fact to be affected by it, the appeal ought to succeed. But "might reasonably affect," that falls far short of the Prosecution's words "would affect." And it highlights the difference, "might reasonably" or "would." Australia, same test, differently worded: "... would have produced a significant possibility that the verdict would have been one of acquittal." Different words mean the same thing. New Zealand: "... might reasonably have led the jury to return different verdicts." The leading case of Dougherty. South Africa: Satisfy the tests. I've copied the leading case, Ndueni and others. "... prima facie likelihood of the truth of the evidence." "... should be materially relevant to the outcome of the trial." Not "would affect the outcome of the trial." Just materially relevant to it. So if I may summarise the effect of the jurisprudence, the common law of England and what was really the old Commonwealth countries have all adopted the test propounded by the appellant for the admission of additional evidence. There is, we submit, conflicting authorities in the United States. None of this is anything more than persuasive. But we would invite the Court to reflect upon the fact that the common law, which is the home of the adversarial system, which is the system that is being operated in this Tribunal, is a highly persuasive -- is highly persuasive jurisprudence when one is considering how to reflect in the Appellate Chamber the same protection against wrongful conviction that must lie at the heart of all criminal justice systems. At the moment you depart from the word "could" or "might" and impose that higher threshold on an appellant of demonstrating that the additional evidence would have resulted in a different verdict, you are opening the door to Appellate Chambers upholding convictions when Trial Chambers, had they had the advantage of hearing the same evidence that the Appeal Chamber had considered, may not and inevitably in some cases would not have convicted. And yet if the respondent's test is to be preferred, those individuals will remain as convicted persons before this Appeal Chamber. In our submission, that would result in a miscarriage of justice as defined -- not defined, as expressed in Article 25 of the Statute, a miscarriage of justice being a conviction recorded against an accused person when the evidence is such that the Trial Chamber might not have convicted. That is, in parenthesis, exactly the test that was annunciated in Stafford and Luvaglio in the House of Lords in England, and in the Supreme Court of New Zealand in the quotation I gave from Mr. Justice Gault. I pause deliberately at this stage of my address to invite whether there are any questions on this particular aspect before I move to consider the question of sentence that I am about to give quite briefly.

utterances.text: Let me inquire of my colleagues. Do we have any questions for Mr. Clegg? I have one, Mr. Clegg. If the "could" or "might" test that you espouse is adopted, would it not be the logical sequence of that that one would invariably remit the case for a new trial to see if the Trial Chamber actually -- what it actually did? Or are you suggesting that if the Appellate Court uses a "might" or "could" test, that if it finds that test satisfied, it will reverse the conviction?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Normally, you would remit for the Trial Chamber to reconsider. Almost inevitably there would be a retrial in light of the new evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. That's basically what I wanted to find out from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Clegg. I think you can proceed with the next aspect of your presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Can I turn, then, to consider the question of sentence. The standard of review has already been the subject of a number of decisions by the Appeals Chamber, and as early in the jurisprudence of the Court in the first appeal Tadic, the Appeal Chamber held that it would not intervene in the exercise of the Trial Chamber's discretion with regard to sentence unless there was "a discernible error." And that test has been followed since then in a number of cases. The effect of that, in practice, has been that those seeking to appeal a sentence have sought to try to identify a particular discernible error in the reasoning of the Trial Chamber such as, for example, the failure to take into account local Yugoslav law or some other factor that is identified in either the Statute or the Rules as a criteria that the Trial Chamber ought to take into account when passing sentence. In the absence of being able to satisfy the Appeal Chamber that there is any error in relation to the Trial Chamber's approach to that issue, then the appeal has failed. In my submission, that's perhaps a rather onerous way of approaching a question of an appeal against sentence. The passing of a sentence in a criminal context is a reflection of the interaction of a large number of different features that combine together to produce the sentence, and the setting of the sentence will necessarily involve the exercise of judgement. By definition, there can be no such thing as the right sentence, and different judges, both acting reasonably, can properly arrive at a different sentence, one from the other. Indeed, one is only to reflect upon exercises that have been conducted of different judges being presented with the facts of a case in isolation, one from the other, to see where a judge has a wide discretion, how the individual sentences of judges practising in the same jurisdiction can sometimes vary considerably. There's nothing wrong in different judges passing different sentences on the same facts. It's inevitable, as long as sentencing is left to the trial judge's discretion. And it's no function of an Appeal Chamber to adjust a reasonable or just sentence to one albeit lower that they would have passed if sitting as members of a Trial Chamber. There ought to be, and I concede, a higher threshold than that. It's no function of this Court just as it won't tinker with a sentence because you think you might have passed one that would have been slightly lower. However, the sentences ought to be the subject of review by this Appeal Chamber. If they are either capricious or perhaps more likely excessive and, in principle, a sentence may be thought to be excessive if it is not of reasonable proportion with a line of sentences passed in similar circumstances for the same offences. And that was the approach of the Appeal Chamber in the recent decision of Jelisic. The importance of that principle is that it opens the door to a fair review of an excessive sentence not by the appellant seeking to identify a discernible error, but by demonstrating that when looked at the case in the round and putting all the factors into account, the sentence is out of reasonable proportion with the line of sentences passed in similar circumstances for the same offences. It is my submission that the number of cases that have now passed through both the Trial Chamber and the Appellate Chamber in this Tribunal, that one is able now to discern a range of sentences or tariff, whatever word one prefers, and can identify, in an appropriate case, an excessive sentence by a comparable exercise with other sentences passed in other cases. It is, in many ways, the fairer approach when you have built up a history of sentencing. It must be fundamentally fair for people who have committed like crimes in like circumstances to receive like sentences. Of course, when the Tribunal first began sitting, there was no yardstick, and one was sentencing very much in a vacuum relying upon the experience of judges to set a sentencing tariff. But as time has passed, we submit the time has now arrived as was really accepted by the Appellate Chamber in Jelisic, time has now come where you can identify, we submit, a discernible pattern of sentencing in this Tribunal. And if sentences are out of line with that and can be demonstrated to be excessive, then that ought to be a ground upon which the sentence ought to be capable of being successfully appealed. Now, in this case, the question arises as to whether the appellants or any of them are able to appeal their sentence on the basis of material that was not advanced before the Trial Chamber because there was no mitigation and, therefore, factors that might ordinarily have been prayed in aid were not advanced. In our submission, the answer to this question is to be found in the Statute of the Tribunal itself. Article 24 sets out various factors that a Trial Chamber is enjoined to take into account before passing sentence. In our submission, it is the duty of the Trial Chamber to satisfy itself that it has that material before it, and if it doesn't, to ensure that, perhaps with the assistance of the Prosecution, if necessary, it is given the factual information necessary in order to give effect to the factors identified in Article 24 prior to the passing of sentence and they include, of course, the individual circumstances of the convicted person. Silence of Defence counsel or silence of an unrepresented defendant does not absolve the Trial Chamber of its obligations under the Statute and under Article 24. It follows from that analysis that if, on appeal, the Trial Chamber can be demonstrated not to have taken account of factors identified by Article 24 and, as a consequence, injustice has resulted, then the Appeal Chamber is certainly entitled, we submit, to review the sentence in the light of that. The alternative would, we submit, be a curious result. Evidence or material placed before the Court in mitigation isn't normally evidence necessarily given on oath, but frequently falls far short of evidence, may amount to reports prepared by doctors, governors of prison, and the like. But that type of material, we submit, can be admitted by an Appeal Chamber in order to assess whether the sentence passed was excessive. If the Appeal Chamber were to shut its eyes to this new material, then the appellant could certainly seek a review under Rule 119 of his sentence assuming, of course, that the material had come to light since his trial. And therefore, we would argue that even if factors emerge after trial, that the Trial Chamber couldn't conceivably have taken into account because the fact may not have existed such as, perhaps, substantial cooperation with the Prosecutor, but at this stage, the Appellate Chamber ought sensibly to take that factor into account when reviewing the sentence rather than close its eyes to it because to do that would merely open the door to a further layer of review as envisaged by Rule 119. It would also, perhaps, be slightly inconsistent if Rule 115 permitted the placing of evidence unavailable at trial before an Appeal Chamber but the material relevant to sentence could not be placed before an Appeal Chamber albeit were to satisfy the same threshold for admissibility. Can I, perhaps, in conclusion, be forgiven for reverting, very briefly, to my earlier submission and just end by indicating that the test that I am seeking to urge for the admission of evidence, namely not "would" but "could" or "might" is, of course, entirely consistent with what the Rules have laid down for the test for review proceedings under Rule 120. What Rule 120 says by way of review is that, "If a majority of Judges of the Chamber that pronounce the judgement agree that the new fact if proved could have been a decisive factor," not would, could, "the Chamber shall review the judgement." Well, it would be absurd if Rule 115 were to set a higher test than Rule 120. That would render the consideration of the evidence by the Trial Chamber a lottery. The lottery being whenever the fact is discovered, you will have potentially a different test to be applied to its admission. I apologise for reverting to that, but I intended to do that earlier. That concludes my submissions of general application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you, indeed, Mr. Clegg. Let me see if my colleagues have any questions on this second aspect. Unfortunately, I have one, that is: Do I understand your argument to be as to sentencing that if a matter was not raised in the trial court in mitigation, that the Appellate Chamber should look at that factor not in the case only of newly-discovered or newly-happened events, but things that were available at the Trial Chamber? In other words, are you suggesting there's a different test for sentencing material that 115 would provide if the material were relevant to the merits of the appeal?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I am. Because the sentencing material is not additional evidence. It's a different category of material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So it's governed not by 115 but by your general justice standard of --

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes. It finds support in Article 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: And the difference being that, of course, the Trial Chamber, when considering evidence that goes to guilt, is entirely dependent upon what evidence the parties places before it. It's under no obligation to go and seek evidence itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Are you suggesting the Trial Chamber or the Appellate Chamber is under such an obligation? For instance, suppose a Defence counsel does not raise anything about individual circumstances which is mentioned in Article 24 in mitigation, are you suggesting that the Appellate Chamber has an obligation to go hunt around and see if there was some mitigating circumstances even though the Defence counsel didn't raise them in the trial court?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Firstly, I'm suggesting the Trial Chamber has that obligation and Article 24 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: How could a Trial Chamber have an obligation to look for individual circumstances if the Defence counsel doesn't raise them?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I have your position. I wanted to make sure I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: My submission is that would apply if Defence counsel were less than helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Clegg. We will now hear, as I understand it, from Mr. Radovic on the vagueness question, and I believe you said you could do your presentation in approximately 30 minutes or less; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: In that case, I think we will have you go ahead and at the end of your 30 minutes which would be approximately 10 minutes after 11.00, we will then have our half an hour break. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our position could be summed up as follows: According to Article 18 of the Statute and the Rule 47(C) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Prosecution has the obligation to include a summary of the facts in the indictment, the summary of the facts on which -- based on which the accused is being charged. We deem that this has not been done which has prevented us from according a fair trial to the accused. The indictment, itself, has two parts; the indictment which was the basis for the trial in this case. That's what I mean. It has been amended -- it was amended immediately before the start of the trial because there was a previous indictment and on the basis of this indictment, the accused voluntarily surrendered to the Court, to the Tribunal. The first part of the indictment contains some vaguely-defined facts. This is the part relating to persecution in which the Kupreskic brothers are charged from persecuting Bosnian Muslims from October 1992 to April 1993 in Ahmici and Santici on political, racial or religious grounds by planning, organising, and implementing an attack which was designed to remove or cleanse all Bosnian Muslims from the village and surrounding areas. It is furthermore alleged that they aided and abetted or participated in the deliberate and systematic killing of Bosnian Muslim civilians, the comprehensive destruction of their homes and property, the organised detention and expulsion of the Bosnian Muslims from Ahmici and Santici. Then, in the previous counts, it is also stated that they took part in military training and were armed, that they evacuated Bosnian Croats the night before the attack, that they organised HVO soldiers and ammunition and weapons in and around the Ahmici village, and that they concealed from the other inhabitants the fact that an attack was forthcoming. In paragraph 400 of the judgement, it is stated that this indictment included the incriminations accepted by the Trial Chamber relating to count H -- to Witness H, but it is obvious from the indictment that no such thing is actually there. We believe that a fair trial entails the knowledge of the accused of the precise charges levied against him which would enable him to defend himself successfully. The different results of the consequences of the two ways in which the indictment was phrased prove that our stand is right. In the first indictment, the accused are charged with events in the -- in Witness KL's house and 10 counts refer to this event. In the first part, the accused were convicted on these charges. And in the second part, which is made more specific and which enabled the accused to defend themselves properly, they were acquitted of these -- on these counts. The fact that this vague indictment, to a certain extent, baffled the Trial Chamber itself can be seen from the Presiding Judge, on two occasions, asked the Prosecutor what is it that he is charging Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic with as regards the events in Witness H's house? One such question was asked in the middle of the Prosecution case, and the other question was asked at the end of the Prosecution case. So if the Presiding Judge of the Trial Chamber that is supposed to pass the judgement in this case, if the Presiding Judge was not quite clear as to what the accused were being charged with, then how could one expect the accused and their Defence counsel to know that, to be clear on that? As regards the demand that the charges be clearly defined, we would like to refer to the Celebici case tried before this Tribunal, IT-96-12-T. In this case, the Trial Chamber found that it would not take into consideration other acts for which evidence had been adduced but which had not been mentioned in the indictment itself. In paragraph 1200 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber states that the Trial Chamber will only limit itself to taking into consideration specific acts alleged in the indictment and will not take into account other acts for the infliction of serious bodily harm and cruel treatment, for which evidence had been adduced in the course of trial but which had not been alleged in the indictment. Therefore, the Trial Chamber will limit itself to considering the factual allegations as they have been stated, and then it goes on to list names which are irrelevant for our present case. This clearly indicates that the final decision rendered by the Trial Chamber was based only on the facts or relating only to the facts where you have specific incriminations. In the same judgement, a Trial Chamber of this Tribunal stated as follows: "The Trial Chamber states that the indictment does not contain allegations pertaining to the incidents described by these witnesses. When evidence was adduced at the trial pertaining to alleged criminal offences not specified in the indictment, the Trial Chamber, for reasons of fairness," And this is a principle that we keep on referring to, "did not consider that unspecified acts can form part of the charges against the accused." We believe that this judgement rendered by this Trial Chamber is a paragon of a legal decision which really accords the accused the rights that they are entitled to in the proceedings; and not only paying lip service to it but really giving them those rights. This would, in brief, be the summary of our view of the indictment. Since we still have some time, if you allow me, I would like to make an addendum to this pertaining to the manner in which the judgement was written or, rather, the way that facts were described therein. When the facts are described in the judgement, there should be a summary of all those things of which the accused has been found guilty. The way in which indictments are written before this Tribunal -- the way in which judgements are written is the following: The Trial Chamber refers to the actual indictment without stating the actual facts, and then they say that the accused is convicted on such and such counts and so on. So they merely use the indictment as it is written, which results in an absurd situation. In the Prosecution count, we have the time period of October 1992 to April 1993. The month of October is taken as the month in which the persecution began. It is done because the first incident in the armed conflict in this area took place then, because there was an incident on a roadblock in Ahmici. The Trial Chamber itself in its judgement specified that this armed conflict was not caused by Croats but by Muslims. If you read the part of the judgement in which convictions are rendered, which accepts the arguments of the Prosecution, then you will think that Croats actually caused the conflict, because not many people go into such detail and will study the judgement in detail. We also have another situation. Under the heading of "Persecution," it is stated that the Kupreskics persecuted Muslims in all the ways as the Prosecution described it in this time period, October 1992, April 1993. And of course you can write down anything, but it is much harder to actually prove it. Yet the Trial Chamber accepted this allegation despite the fact that on page 6094 of the Trial Chamber, we have an allegation made by the Prosecution indicating that it is stipulated that until the 16th of April, the Kupreskics were good people and good neighbours. So the Prosecution stipulates this, indicating that they were not engaged in the acts of persecution that they are being charged with. This will be more or less what I have to say now, although I will speak in some detail about other problems relating to facts. Unless you want me to go on now, because I still have some time. One of the basic principles of the proceedings, as guaranteed by the Statute, is that everybody is considered equal before this Tribunal, which means that every accused has to be treated in the same way. Yet the Tribunal does not act in this way, because some pieces of evidence -- there is an exhibit offered by the Prosecution, P355. This is a list of members of the Home Guard Regiment. And there is also a time period in which these people were actually members of this Home Guard Regiment. The Defence counsel challenged the authenticity of this document, but this is besides the point. I will come back to that. As regards Dragan Papic, a co-accused in the same proceedings who was acquitted, the Trial Chamber accepted the view of the Defence counsel for Dragan Papic, accepting that the people who took part in the war were given certain privileges. So the Trial Chamber accepted the validity of this document as regards the Kupreskic brothers, yet stated that it was not authentic as regards Dragan Papic. Also, it is stated for one of the accused that he was a good man and a good neighbour until April 1993. They accepted this fact in his case but refused to accept the same fact in mitigation as regards the Kupreskic brothers. Also, it is also accepted that they organised HVO soldiers and weapons and ammunition around the Ahmici and Santici village. There is no evidence to support this fact, and the Trial Chamber does not even state that this fact has been proven. Furthermore, it is stated that they supported, in the time period from October, the systematic killing of Muslim civilians, destruction of Muslim houses and property, organised the detention of Muslims, and so on and so forth. As regards these two, there is nothing said in support of this in the judgement, yet there cannot be because it is well known that they have been good neighbours and good people up until April 1993. What we would like to know is how can the Trial Chamber use the allegations in the indictment as the basis for their judgement, yet in the same judgement also refute the allegations in the indictment? I would not like to waste any more of your time, Your Honours. I think that I have said all that I needed to say at this point.
