utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Wald, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the topic I shall Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. deal with in this brief space of time is doubtless very significant and comprehensive. When one considers what should be said in this brief period of time, one has to judge what is essential, what is important, and what is less important and need not be said here. What we heard in my learned friend Mr. Clegg's presentation is certainly something we all agree with. We did not have very detailed consultations, and each one of us feels we could add something. The matters that this International Tribunal deals with show this clearly. When discussing sentencing, we can view this either from the aspect of the jurisprudence of the Tribunal or the aspect of legislation. I shall deal with matters pertaining to the jurisprudence of the courts of the former Yugoslavia, but first let me say a few words by way of introduction to show how important this topic was and how many dilemmas there were as to whether this International Tribunal is bound to respect the provisions in Rule 101 and in Article 24 of the Statute that the -- one of the things to be taken into account is the general practice regarding prison sentences in the courts of the former Yugoslavia. This is not a topic I shall be discussing, but it seems to me that a comprehensive interpretation of Article 24 of the Statute of the Tribunal, not just the key words contained in Articles -- or in subparagraphs 1 or 2 that this shall be taken into account, but also part 3 of this Rule which deals with compensation. It seems to me that the Security Council wished to say that this practice can be taken account, but need not be taken into account. But as I say, this is not a topic I shall be discussing at great length. However, it seems to me that this is was the intention. Let us now go back to the question of the jurisprudence of the courts of the former Yugoslavia as one of the relevant circumstances which the Court should consider. We must ask what jurisprudence you are actually referring to. Is there no precedent for this Tribunal to refer to the jurisprudence of a national court? I think not. Because as I understand it, the decisions reached here must first of all bear a message for the lands of the former Yugoslavia, and this is one of the things that was expressed in the Security Council resolution because one of the purposes of this Tribunal is the restoration of peace and peaceful coexistence on the territory of the former Yugoslavia. What are the basic tenets one should start from? Is this Tribunal bound to take into consideration the jurisprudence of the former Yugoslavia or is it to be used only as something to be considered? The courts of the former Yugoslavia primarily founded their decisions on certain principles, and before I start dealing with specific pragmatic issues, let me say the following: In the light of these, one can consider what circumstances this Tribunal has taken into account. The Penal Code of the former Yugoslavia started from the fact that criminal responsibility is the basis of sentencing. We shall see that at this Tribunal, the emphasis was laid on the gravity of the offence. However, when taking into consideration all the circumstances, the criminal responsibility must also be taken into account as it was in the courts of the former Yugoslavia because however serious the offence, there will be no punishment if there is no criminal responsibility. The second principle which should be kept in mind is that the courts in the former Yugoslavia abandoned the system whereby strict rules are laid down stating what concrete circumstances must effect the length of the sentence. According to the rules contained in this law, it should be mentioned that the law provided only for a general framework for sentencing, and it was left up to the court to take into consideration all the circumstances of a specific case and to pronounce an individual sentence. It is important to point out, bearing in mind the overall practice of sentencing of the courts of the former Yugoslavia, that courts could also pronounce a sentence that fell outside the prescribed framework if the court found -- deemed it necessary to do so in a particular case. So these were only some general observations regarding the sentencing practice of the courts of the former Yugoslavia. What relevant provisions should this Tribunal, if it decides that this is helpful, rely on? The Penal Code of the former Yugoslavia contained some general rules of sentencing in Article 41, and besides this, there were some special rules regarding sentencing for concurrent criminal offences. Then it contained special rules on sentencing below a certain minimum, and mitigating or aggravating circumstances. In all this, it is important to stress that these general rules were binding upon the courts in the former Yugoslavia to pronounce sentencing within the framework of the law bearing in mind the purpose of the punishment which was, on the one hand, general prevention and to deter potential criminals, and to influence people not to commit criminal offences and to strengthen, discipline, responsibility, respect for the law. As can be seen in some of the judgements passed by this Tribunal, retribution was not an element to be considered in sentencing. When the court sentenced persons under this law, it also took into consideration the individual circumstances which led to the sentence being higher or lower within the prescribed limits. The courts in Yugoslavia took into consideration the degree of criminal responsibility, which was a very important circumstance; the motives for the offence; the previous history and the conduct of the accused and of the sentenced person and other circumstances. These are just some examples. But the court could take into consideration any circumstance that it found helpful in evaluating the sentence that was most suitable for that offence. In some decisions of high courts in the former Yugoslavia, it was stated that this sentence had to be a result of all the circumstances and not just some of them. It should also be pointed out when discussing this jurisprudence, is the question of those circumstances that constitute elements of the criminal offence cannot then be considered again as aggravating circumstances, because the law built these circumstances into the offence itself. Also, those elements which surpassed the extent of elements constituting a crime were to be taken into account in sentences. So these provisions of Article 41 of the Penal Code of the former Yugoslavia set out only the most typical circumstances to be taken into account, but the court was free to take into account other circumstances also. When considering the degree of criminal responsibility, these issues mainly came down to evaluating the ability of the perpetrator to understand the crime and to control his actions. They evaluated a whole range of states of mind of the person, taking into account the opinion of psychiatrists. At one extreme were persons who were fully aware of the meaning of their acts; at the other end of the scale were those who were totally unable to comprehend this. Then there was also the question of guilt. And in various places in the law, both of these elements were taken into account, but when sentencing, they had to be seen together. In evaluating this circumstance, the practice of the courts concentrated mainly on the issue of premeditation, direct premeditation, where the perpetrator is fully aware of the consequences of his acts and he willingly commits it, or where the perpetrator was aware but did not want the circumstances to happen. Then there is also negligence. So there is conscious and unconscious negligence. The degree of criminal liability and its evaluation was one of the factors taken into account in sentencing. The motive for the crime was also a very significant circumstance which was, in some cases, taken as an aggravating factor, and in other circumstances, as an aggravating factor; whether the criminal offence was accompanied by hatred, revenge, wishful material gain or whether the person was in some way forced to act as he did. So all this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting. I'm sorry, Mr. Pavkovic. I just wanted to remind you you've got just a few more minutes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I forgot myself a little because of my colleagues. So the circumstances under which the offence was committed were taken into account and were reflected in the sentencing practice of the courts. The previous history of the convicted person and his bearing after the commission of the crime, this was also relevant in selecting a sentence; whether the accused later showed signs of remorse or offered to make up for the damage, and so on. The bearing of the accused during the trial was also taken as an important circumstance, whether he surrendered, whether he was cooperative. So all this was taken in mitigation. And to conclude an admission of guilt, if it was complete and sincere, and if it helped to throw light on the act, was also taken in mitigation. However, failure to confess and denial of the act was not taken as an aggravating circumstance because the perpetrator is not bound to testify against himself. So this is just a general overview of the sentencing practice of the courts of the former Yugoslavia, and if it can help, together with all the other circumstances to be taken into account, then this modest contribution will have been useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Pavkovic. Do we have any questions? No. Thank you. Next on the agenda is the Prosecution's appeal against the conviction and sentence, and I think, Mr. Yapa, at our Status Conference you asked for 15 minutes for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: It is 15 minutes, and Ms. Suominen will deal with the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOELAERT-SUOMINEN
utterances.text: Madam President, honourable members of the Chamber, my name is Sonja Boelaert-Souminen. May we now present the Prosecution's own appeal in this case. As you have gathered from our submission at the Status Conference, our submissions will be brief, mainly for the reasons that we believe that our arguments and authorities have been reasonably supported by jurisprudence coming out from the Appeals Chamber. My oral argument will be structured as follows: After a brief introduction, I will also go very briefly over the procedural history of our own appeal. Then I will go over to the main points of the Prosecution's own appeal in this case, and this consists of question of cumulative charging on the one hand and the question of cumulative conviction on the other. I will then conclude our submissions on the Prosecution's own appeal in this case, and then I will briefly elaborate on an additional error in sentencing which the Prosecution submits the Trial Chamber committed in relation to one of the accused persons. And finally, I will end my submissions with restating the relief sought by the Prosecution in relation to its own appeal in this case. The Prosecution's own appeal in this case is limited to the verdict on two of the charges laid against each of the following two persons: Drago Josipovic and Vladimir Santic. When you read the indictment, you will see that these two persons had been charged with multiple crimes arising out of the same acts. The conduct the accused has been charged with is set out in paragraphs 32 through 35 of the indictment. The cumulative convictions I am going to deal with today relate all events surrounding the killing of Musafer Puscul and the burning of the Puscul home. For their role in the killing of Musafer Puscul, the accused had been charged with the count of murder under Article 3 of the Statute which refers to common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions, but also under Article 5 of the Statute as a crime against humanity. For the conduct which consisted of forcibly removing the Puscul family from their home and holding the family members nearby, by killing Musafer Puscul and burning the family home, the two accused persons had been charged with a count of cruel treatment under Article 3 of the Statute, and a count of inhumane acts under Article 5 of the Statute. The Trial Chamber found that the Prosecution had established the facts beyond a reasonable doubt. The Trial Chamber also found that the Prosecution had proven the culpable role played by these two accused persons in these events. Finally, the Trial Chamber found that the facts as proven met the elements of the different crimes they had been charged with. However, the Trial Chamber found, for reasons of law, that the war crimes charges, and I'm referring here to the Article 3 charges, had been improperly charged cumulatively with the more serious offences under Article 5 of the Statute. The Trial Chamber based this decision on its analysis of the principles of concurrence of offences, and this is set out in paragraphs 637 through 748 of the judgement. In conclusion, the Trial Chamber decided that the prohibition of murder as a crime against humanity was lex specialis in relation to the prohibition of murder as a violation of the laws and customs of war and it followed the same reasoning for the multiple charges of cruel treatment and inhumane acts. The Trial Chamber decided to dismiss the counts based on Article 3 of the Statute and find the two accused not guilty under these war crimes charges. The Prosecution filed its appeals brief in this case on the 3rd of July of the year 2000. At that time, the question of concurrence of offences had arisen in one other case before the Appeals Chamber in this case. I'm referring to the Celebici case. By the time it came to file the respondents' briefs, the Prosecution noted that the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal had rendered an important judgement dealing, for the first time, with some of the principles relating to concurrence of offences. I'm referring here to the Celebici appeals judgment which was rendered on the 20th of February of this year. Shortly after the Celebici appeals judgement was rendered, two Trial Chambers sitting in other cases rendered a judgement whereby they applied the test articulated by this Celebici appeals judgement in relation to pairs of commitive [sic] convictions which were issued in both cases. I'm referring to the Kunarac judgement which was rendered on the 22nd of February of this year, and also to the Kordic and Cerkez judgement which was rendered on the 26th of February of this year. Because the Prosecution believed that this jurisprudence constituted significant developments in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, that the Prosecution sought leave to file an amended appeals brief in this case. Leave was granted, and the Prosecution filed an amended appeals brief in this case on the 15th of May of this year. By the time the Prosecution had arrived to file its replies briefs to the two respondents' briefs filed in this case, this Appeals Chamber had rendered a further judgement dealing with the question of concurrence of offences, and this is the Jelisic judgement rendered on the 5th of July of the year 2001. The Prosecution took the opportunity to take account of this new development or this further jurisprudence in its prior briefs to the respondents' briefs filed by -- on behalf of the persons Drago Josipovic and Vladimir Santic. The Prosecution submits that it has discussed this jurisprudence in detail both in its amended appeals brief and in its reply briefs, and I will not, therefore, go into detail today. I will just -- would like to draw Your Honours' attention, if I may, to the main points of the Prosecution's appeal in this case. The criticism by the Prosecution of the judgement rendered in this case insofar as the question of concurrence of offences is concerned is basically threefold. The Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber firstly incorrectly set out and further incorrectly applied the legal principles applicable to the question of cumulative charges in this Tribunal. Secondly, the Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber incorrectly applied the legal principles applicable to the question of cumulative convictions in the legal system of this Tribunal, in particular, insofar as the question of multiple convictions between Article 3 and Article 5 is concerned. Thirdly, and consequently, the Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber's decision to acquit the respondents on Counts 17 and 19 of the indictment which refer to the war crimes characters is invalid, is an error of law under Article 25(1)(a) of the Statute. The first point of the Prosecution as set out previously is that the Trial Chamber incorrectly set out and applied the principles relating to the practice of cumulative charges in this Tribunal. This question, we submit, has been dealt with by the Celebici appeals judgement and more, in particular, paragraph 400 of this judgement. In the Celebici appeals judgement, this Appeals Chamber for the first time rendered a decision relating to the question of concurrence of offences whereas the Celebici appeals judgement decided that the question of cumulative convictions could only be allowed, that the practice of cumulative convictions could only be allowed under certain circumstances of which I will talk later. The appeals judgement decided that the practice of cumulative charges, on the other hand, should be generally allowed for the following reasons, and I'm reading here part of paragraph 400 of the Celebici judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I do want to remind you that you've got about 5 minutes left if there are certain points that you want to be sure that you are able to cover.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOELAERT-SUOMINEN
utterances.text: I will not read paragraph 400 of the Celebici appeals judgement, but I will just add that in relation to this decision, we believe that the Trial Chamber's decision was in error. With respect to the question of cumulative convictions, Your Honours, we believe that not only the Celebici appeals judgement but, in particular, the Jelisic appeals judgement which was rendered recently on the 5th of July of the year 2000 fully supports the arguments and authorities developed by the Prosecution in its amended appeal brief and in its reply briefs which were filed recently. The Celebici appeals judgement decided that cumulative convictions between multiple charges in the indictment can be allowed under the following circumstances when you are dealing with generally distinct offences under international criminal law. In order to determine whether one is dealing with generally distinct offences, the test is what I would call the different elements test. If each of the crimes at issue contain a materially distinct element not contained in the other. When we filed our amended appeals brief in this case, the Prosecution submitted that cumulative convictions between Article 3 and Article 5 should be generally allowed because the test was met. And the distinct material element which, according to the Prosecution, is contained in the Article 3 charges is the question of -- factor that there needs to be a closed or sufficient nexus with armed conflict. The distinct material element contained in Article 5 offences, according to the Prosecution, was the requirement that the crimes against humanity for a part of a widespread or systematic campaign against the civilian population, and we believe that the Jelisic appeals judgement confirms that the arguments developed by the Prosecution in this regard are legally sound. The Jelisic appeals judgement, first of all, is relevant because it deals with the same categories of offences; Article 3 and Article 5 offences. Secondly, because it also deals with the same, exactly the same offences as those that are at issue in the case at bar: Murder under Article 3, murder under Article 5; cruel treatment under Article 3, inhumane acts under Article 5. Thirdly the Jelisic appeals judgement confirms that there are no cogent reasons in the interests of justice which would justify a departure from this jurisprudence. In the fourth place, we believe that the Jelisic appeals judgement is relevant because it confirms that in order to determine whether there are distinct legal elements one should only look at the elements that go into the actus reus or the mens rea of the offence but it can also take into account the jurisdictional elements or contextual elements. In conclusion, Your Honour, the relief sought by the Prosecution is that the Appeals Chamber, first of all, note the errors which are contained in the judgement under appeal, and I'm not going to repeat the errors. The basis of the relief sought by the Prosecution is that the Appeals Chamber reverse the acquittals of Drago Josipovic and Vladimir Santic on Counts 17 and 19 of the indictment and find the accused guilty on these counts. Finally Your Honour, if you allow me one more minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: One minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOELAERT-SUOMINEN
utterances.text: As set out in our amended appeals brief, the Prosecution submits that there is an additional error in sentencing committed by the Trial Chamber in relation to the accused Drago Josipovic. When you read the sentencing part, you will note that Drago Josipovic received a sentence of 15 years for the count of murder but a sentence of 10 years for the count of persecution. Whilst the Prosecution believes that the total sentence handed down against the accused Drago Josipovic is appropriate in view of the severity of his conduct, the Prosecution submits that the way the sentencing was set out is, nonetheless, in error for the reason that the underlying conduct which was taken into account for the count of murder also formed the basis of the underlying conduct of the persecution charge. However, the persecution charge was based on a much wider set of facts in relation to Drago Josipovic. It took into account, for instance, Drago Josipovic's role in relation to victim Nazif Ahmic. This, Your Honours, if there are no questions from the Bench in relation to my submission, would conclude the Prosecution's own appeal in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Suominen. Do we have any questions? I just want to verify one thing. You are not, I gather, you are not asking for any new sentencing in regard to Article 3, Article 5, if your position prevails on appeal, all other things being equal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOELAERT-SUOMINEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is our submission. We're only asking for reversal of the acquittals, not for an increase in sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOELAERT-SUOMINEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: We will now, because it is -- yes, we will now, because it is 12.10, and with Mr. Abell's consent, we will begin with his argument. He may not be able to complete it, because I think we will -- he has a total -- we will have lunch. So I would advise him in advance that he has a total of 85 minutes; that's the same that's given to all the appellants. So I would see 45 minutes of that taking us to 1.00, at which time, if he can conclude in that vicinity, we'll be able to break for lunch and he can finish after lunch. Go ahead. I'm also going to take 30 seconds, Mr. Abell, and just alert you to just two points that I think would be useful. You may intend to cover them in your argument anyway. Those would be exactly what bearing you think the findings of Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic's police role had on the overall findings of the Trial Chamber, and what impact you think the evidence of AT would have on his appeal. Go ahead till approximately 1.00 or in that vicinity, whenever you want to break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, we arrive mercifully ahead of schedule to look at the appeal of Vlatko Kupreskic, and I hope I don't make a rash promise, but I will do my level best to make sure that whilst I'm on my feet the momentum will be kept up. I stress, I hope that isn't a rash promise. On his behalf, we have filed the following pleadings: the appellant's brief on the 5th of September of last year, now public in its redacted form; the supplemental appellant's brief filed on the 12th of June of this year; and a reply to the Prosecution respondent's brief filed on the 18th of July. Those written pleadings, we hope, set out the arguments which we put forward on behalf of Vlatko Kupreskic, and they deal, we hope, with the issues in very considerable detail. Now, the purpose of what I have to say on his behalf now, in this oral argument, is not, of course, to slavishly repeat what is already set out in the pleadings, but it is my opportunity, I hope in this speech, to complement those pleadings by drawing some of the threads together and commenting on the impact of the various segments of evidence which we have heard, and factoring it into the evidence upon which this appellant Vlatko Kupreskic was convicted. I will focus, I hope, on what we perceive to be the major issues. But may I stress before I leave these introductory remarks that we rely, of course, as we always have done, on our written pleadings, and I'm sure that they will be considered by Your Honours in conjunction with the oral arguments we present. The submissions that I'm going to start, then, will be divided into seven chapters. The first chapter will deal briefly with the Trial Chamber's legal findings and comment upon the nature of the Prosecution's case upon which the appellant Vlatko Kupreskic was convicted. Chapters 2 to 6 will deal with the various segments of the evidence both called at trial and additional evidence heard by this Appeals Chamber. And Chapter 7, which, because by then I feel that you will deserve a change of voice, my learned co-counsel Mr. Livingston will present, that will be the sentencing appeal. It will be necessary for me, when dealing with parts of Chapters 2 to 6, to go into private session. I will indicate just before that is necessary when it is necessary, and I hope it won't cause any difficulty. Can I simply say this before moving on to the first chapter: Concerning the standard of review, we adopt the submissions which were advanced this morning by Mr. Clegg; in other words, in a sentence, the correct test is "might" or "could the additional evidence have caused a reasonable Trial Chamber to have come to a different verdict?" And, again, we repeat what we set out in our supplemental appellant's brief, page 3, at paragraph 8. Chapter 1, then, the Trial Chamber's findings, I summarise them, I hope, briefly. They are to be found at paragraphs 795 to 804 of the Trial Chamber's judgement, and they are (a) to (f); that the appellant was a member of the police, an operations officer for the prevention of crimes of particular state interest with the rank of inspector first class; that his role was more than merely a maker of an inventory at the Vitez Police Station; (b) that he was unloading weapons from a car in front of his home in October of 1992, and that there was sightings of him in and around his house and the Sutra shop on the afternoon, early evening of the 15th of April of 1993, the eve of the attack on Ahmici; (c) that an identification of him in front of the Hotel Vitez on the morning of the 15th of April was held to be correct; (d) that there was an entry in Witness V's diary recording that an information had been -- or that he had learned that Croats were concentrating around the Kupreskic houses; (e) that the evidence of Witness H as to the appellant's presence nearby to the home of Suhret Ahmic in the early hours of the morning of the 16th; although there was no evidence as to what he was actually doing, it was concluded that he was present, ready to lend assistance in whatever way he could. And from that it was deduced that the appellant was involved in the preparations for the attack on Ahmici in his role as police operations officer, and by agreeing to the use of his house as a strategic point and staging area for the attacking troops. That is a summary of the legal findings late on in the judgement. However, in our contention, it is perhaps instructive to see the process by which the Trial Chamber came to arrive at those legal findings, and that appears somewhat earlier in the judgement at -- I give you the reference; I certainly don't ask anyone necessarily to turn it up. But it's at page 176 of the judgement, "Findings of the Trial Chamber in Relation to Vlatko Kupreskic." In our submission, the reading in particular of paragraphs 462 through to 471, which demonstrates perhaps the reasoning and thought process that lay behind arriving at those findings, is set out. It, I submit, makes instructive reading because it demonstrates how the Trial Chamber, having made, for example, one finding of fact, for example, that Vlatko Kupreskic worked for the police between 1992 and 1993, making that finding of fact as being more than an inventory compiler, use that finding as strong support upon which another or other findings could be made. And in particular, I refer to the judgement, using that example, at paragraph 463. I just quote briefly a segment from that paragraph: "The Trial Chamber rejects the evidence of the accused to the effect that he was concerned merely to make inventories of supplies for the police and finds that he was an active operations officer." Finding. "This occupation explains why he was seen unloading weapons from a car in front of his house in October 1992, and was again seen there on the afternoon of the 15th of April, 1993," that all being evidence which the Trial Chamber accepts. That which was found proved against Vlatko Kupreskic, Count 1, aiding and abetting persecution, was based, we contend, in general terms, upon various disparate pieces of evidence which can, for the most part, if not completely, be fairly described as circumstantial evidence from which the Trial Chamber felt able, on the information that they had, to draw certain inferences and conclusions. Again, going back to paragraphs 462 through to 471, the phrase "The Trial Chamber concludes from the above evidence that ..." appears many times - paragraph 466, by way of example; paragraph 470 - reaching a conclusion on a piece of circumstantial evidence and using it to knit together with other circumstantial evidence to, as it were, found the basis upon which he was convicted of aiding and abetting on Count 1. Now, we submit, although of course it's a perfectly legitimate exercise and can be done by courts, to take disparate pieces of evidence and assess their cumulative effect, nonetheless - I'll have more to say about that later - these disparate pieces of circumstantial evidence, we submit, when taken individually and in isolation, could not prove this appellant's complicity even as an aider and abettor. It is only if those disparate pieces of evidence are treated, as they were by the Trial Chamber, as mutually dependent; that anything like enough material upon which to sustain a conviction is seen. And I come back to the example at paragraph 463 of the judgement. If I can draw an analogy, the evidence which was accepted as proof of Vlatko Kupreskic's guilt can perhaps be likened to a spider's web, a spider's web which has just a few strands, all of which support each other and each of which supports the whole structure. It's a delicate thing, is a spider's web, just as in our submission, the evidence against Vlatko Kupreskic can fairly be described as tenuous. And if one, or two, or three of those seven strands are taken away, are neutralised or explained then, in our submission, not I hope pushing the analogy too far, the spider's web simply disintegrates and there isn't the material upon which a conviction can be sustained. That is why we have described in ground of appeal A that the evidence is fairly described against this man as tenuous. Of course the whole point in many ways of circumstantial evidence is that the more information you have, the better position you are in to evaluate the strengths on one side or, other side of the coin, the limitations of that circumstantial evidence. Can I draw another little analogy? I hope that the last, just to bring the point home, a crossword analogy. It's not intended to be a particularly profound one, but it's just to explain how fresh facts can put evidence, circumstantial evidence, in a completely new light. If one has a four-word include a clue in a crossword puzzle and one can't quite get the answer, but one has a hunch that the answer is "best," b-e-s-t, it's consistent with the clue, and it's the strong hunch that it's going to be "best." When one suddenly gets the clue going the opposite way, one finds out that what one needs to have in the third letter is an "S" turns out to be "L," it cannot be "best," it must be "belt." A rather frivolous example, but just showing how fresh information in the form of another clue can completely change the evaluation, the weight that can be placed on disparate pieces of evidence. And we submit in this case is that that is what we have done in this appeal. The additional evidence which we have called or which is there for evaluation by the Appeals Chamber casts new light upon those seven strands, as it were, of the spider's web upon the disparate pieces of substantial evidence upon by Vlatko Kupreskic's conviction was based. And we submit that they strongly assist, they put this Appeals Chamber in a much better position to see the fuller picture to evaluate, to recognise the limitations of the evidence upon which this conviction was based. I revisit, briefly, that paragraph 463 of the judgement where it was said that, "Because the Trial Chamber found that Vlatko Kupreskic worked for the police," as it says, "in 1992 and 1993, that explains the sighting of him or the alleged sighting of him as removing weapons from his vehicle in October of 1992." The difficulty about that when we look at it is this: Firstly, the unloading of the weapons in October 1992 looked at in isolation, that it really is a straw in the wind. I saw that for this reason: How can - - I pose this rhetorical question - how can a sighting of allegedly unloading weapons in October 1992 fully six months before the conflict in Ahmici in April of 1993 and, what is more, at a time when the tension in the Vitez area which, of course, includes the village of Ahmici was between Croats and Serbs as opposed to Croats and Muslims, how can that piece of evidence, by itself, really be a satisfactory basis upon which to conclude fully six months later, in a completely different tense situation, this man was involved in the preparations for the conflict? It is, in our submission, it cannot be used in that way taken by itself. It is simply too remote. But, of course, it was, as it were, latched on to by the Trial Chamber when taken into conjunction with the deduction that this man worked at a higher grade in the police than was originally suggested. What was that deduction based on? It was based purely on two paper exhibits, Exhibit 377 and Exhibit 378 put in broad terms supporting the contention that Vlatko Kupreskic had been an active operations officer. Now, the difficulty, of course, with that conclusion on the two pieces of paper is this: That the Trial Chamber did not have the advantage that Your Honours in the Appeals Chamber have of having heard the evidence of ADB, ADC, and Miro Lazarevic, all Rule 115 additional evidence witnesses who were able to speak in their separate ways in some depth about those pieces of paper, about what Vlatko Kupreskic really did at the police station and, indeed, that, of course, he wasn't working for the police in October of 1992 when that alleged sighting was made in relation to the weapons. So that's, I hope, an example of the limitations of that type of evidence and knitting two pieces of evidence together in that way when one doesn't have the full picture as we submit the Trial Chamber didn't. And we make this further general observation that in this appeal, Vlatko Kupreskic genuinely stands apart from the other appellants, really for two reasons we make that submission. Firstly, the tenuous evidence which resulted in his conviction, and secondly, because in his appeal, there genuinely is a substantial body of additional evidence upon which one can evaluate and see more clearly the limitations of the circumstantial evidence available at that stage on its own to the Trial Chamber. The additional evidence called, if I can analyse it very briefly in this way, goes to four of the legal findings. It leaves aside -- and the seventh legal finding is no more than, as it were, a deduction from the other six. So in a sense it's six legal findings rather than seven. The other two are B and E which, we submit, when looked at on their own, are insufficient to sustain this conviction and which, in the course of argument later on, I will deal with on its -- on their merits. I come now to chapter 2 and I'm going to touch now on matters where it may be wiser, Your Honours, to go into, if we could, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, before we do that, and we certainly will accommodate that in the interests of witness protection, can you give me an estimate of how long we're likely to be in private session on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: That's, if I may say so, a very good question. I would have thought possibly up until -- possibly up until the luncheon adjournment, quite possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Do you think you can cover all of the private session so that for the convenience of everybody when we reassemble, we can be back in public session?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. I do hope so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Madam Registrar, can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: When I say this, I certainly don't mean it offensively to anybody, but perhaps Witness ADA has generated more heat than light in as far as the respondent's brief is concerned. Forgive me, but peppered as it is with subjective comments as to that particular witness, we have done our best, on behalf of Vlatko Kupreskic in the pleadings that we have made, to be objective, realistic, and clinical in the pleadings that we make. Features of his evidence and the witnesses called by the Prosecution to rebut him have been extensively argued in the pleadings, and I don't intend to take up time by rehearsing those detailed arguments now. I don't believe in the time available to me I could do them justice. I'm going, instead, to try to restrict myself to making some, as it were, headline points about Witness ADA. These may be, not exhaustively, but these may be the key points as far as he is concerned. Firstly, it's important, we submit, if I can use this slang phrase for a moment, to keep one's eye on the ball - I'm perhaps mixing my similes or metaphors - and to look at the overall picture. Let us not forget that Witness ADA, both in a statement which was available at the trial and in the evidence that he gave on the Rule 115 hearing, incriminated two other people in the dock in this appeal. We submit that it is difficult to see why he should do any such thing if he has come to this court to lie. It is, secondly, important to remember that ADA was a Muslim whose family were victims in the appalling events which took place on the 16th of April. He lost his own father in what took place. It is again, we submit, difficult to see why he should come to this court to lie about somebody who, if he is telling deliberate lies, he would presumably know to be guilty of the crime of which he was convicted. Those two difficulties are easily resolved, in our submission, if one looks at ADA in the way that we ask Your Honours to do. The answer becomes very simple if one concludes that the reason he is here is because he's come here to tell the truth. If somebody did something and he knows it and they're guilty of something, he doesn't shy away from saying so; alternatively, if someone isn't or wasn't where they were allegedly sighted, he doesn't shy away from saying that either. It may well be that he is a man whom some would say has an, to put it mildly, eccentric manner. But in our submission, witnesses can be eccentric. Witnesses can sometimes be colourful in the way they describe incidents, maybe even sometimes exaggerate, for example, drunkenness or behaviour, but that doesn't mean that on fundamental issues, they haven't come to this Court to tell the truth. And that is how we ask Witness ADA to be viewed. If he is or may be telling the truth, then he, too, thoroughly undermines the evidence of L, M, and O, and supports the evidence of the witness that I dealt with in the last chapter on this topic. The Prosecution, in their response, seek to, as it were, divide and conquer in their assessment of ADA and AT. I'll deal with it, I believe I can deal with it in this way, they -- their argument runs thus: If soldiers were seen by ADA late at night on the 15th of April as, according to AD they were, in the cluster of houses which include Branko Kupreskic house, I stress again, a distance away from Vlatko Kupreskic's house, that, they say, doesn't sit well a AT's evidence. That's why I say "divide and conquer." However, the real analysis, we submit, of the position is this: Start by considering what was the evidence which went towards Vlatko Kupreskic's conviction on Count 1 in relation to soldiers? The evidence upon which he was convicted was the sighting by L, M and O, principally L, of soldiers outside his, Vlatko Kupreskic's house, at dusk at about 6.00 to 6.30 p.m., not soldiers outside Branko's garage, a cluster of houses apart from Vlatko Kupreskic's, several hours later. ADA's sighting of the soldier at Branko's garage does not, on that analysis, assist the Prosecution one jot as regards the appeal of Vlatko Kupreskic. To put it very simply, it's a sighting in the wrong place and at the wrong time as regards the material upon which Vlatko Kupreskic was convicted. As regards Witness L, not only is there the evidence, the additional evidence which casts grave doubt upon the circumstances of the sighting of the soldiers and Vlatko Kupreskic, and I refer to AT and ADA, but there have to be added -- this is the last part of this chapter before we rise for the luncheon adjournment -- there has to be added these other factors. Firstly, the Prosecution's decision which remains an unexplained position as to why he was not called, this is Witness L, to deal with what he said about the defendant who was acquitted, Papic, in relation to a charge of murder no less where a clear statement from L implicating Papic in the murder was available. For some reason, and we simply don't know why, the Prosecution decided not to call L on that. We submit this: that that must cause a question mark to loom large over L. Secondly, and this is more a point on the evidence, it's an identification point. The situation is this: L claimed to have seen Vlatko Kupreskic together with Mirko Vidovic and another outside his house at about dusk -- outside the shop, sorry, at about dusk just a few yards away from the house, on the evening of the 15th, the early evening of the 15th. That identification heavily disputed by Vlatko Kupreskic, was relied upon by the Prosecution. This is the point. The Defence at trial were able to prove, we submit, beyond paraventia that Mirko Vidovic simply could not have been there. Documents were produced at trial, an HVO travel permit, his passport with stamps in it, and a certificate from Frankfurt which comprehensively established that at the material time, Mirko Vidovic was in Germany and therefore could not have been sitting outside the Sutra shop next to Vlatko Kupreskic's house in Ahmici. Now, in our submission, bearing in mind that Mirko Vidovic is another close neighbour, someone who would have been known well to L, bearing in mind that it was not challenged as things turned out in the trial that that was correct, that Mirko Vidovic was, in fact, in Germany, we are left with this situation: A disputed identification of Vlatko Kupreskic by L made at the same time as effectively an admitted misidentification of somebody that L knows just as well as Vlatko Kupreskic. That, alone, must cast considerable doubt upon the correctness and reliability of L's disputed identification of Vlatko Kupreskic. It is noteworthy, of course we accept that not every single last subclause of evidence needs to be trotted out in a judgement, it is worthy of note, perhaps, that this was a pretty important point, this Mirko Vidovic misidentification, and it did not find its way into the judgement of the Trial Chamber. We submit that that is, perhaps, significant. He was, we submit, a central witness to the proper evaluation of the purported identification by Witness L. I hope that's a convenient moment. That's the end of Chapter 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. That's a most convenient moment. By my reckoning, you have about 35 minutes left for your case when you return. We would now adjourn for lunch until 2.30. utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, all. Mr. Abell, I think you have about 35 minutes left for either you or your worthy co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Chapter 4 on my submissions on the appeal against conviction deals with other miscellaneous evidence called by the Prosecution. Witness B, first of all, a disputed sighting of Vlatko Kupreskic outside the Hotel Vitez on the 15th of April. In our contention, great care should be taken with this piece of evidence. On the face of it, taken by itself, it is not, in our submission, evidence which is capable of proving guilt against the appellant Vlatko Kupreskic, especially given that Vlatko Kupreskic's Sutra supermarket as opposed to the shop warehouse in Ahmici, a supermarket in Vitez is literally just down the road in Vitez, nearby to the police station. It discloses no, if I can put it this way, guilty activity on the part of Vlatko Kupreskic. Of course, he disputed at trial, as he still does, his presence there at that time, on that day. It is, we submit, a problematic piece of evidence of a classic, fleeting glance or fleeting glimpse identification, with all the safeguards which are required in the leading case which is in our bundle of authorities, which I won't refer to in extenso, of the Queen against Turnbull, a leading case in English jurisdiction, as to how identification evidence should be approached by a fact-finding tribunal. It was an observation in a moving vehicle in difficult circumstances, some 30 yards distant from the person said to be observed. Hardly ideal circumstances, we submit, in which to make a reliable identification. Witness KL, a disputed sighting of Vlatko Kupreskic on a road on the 15th of April. KL, of course, made another purported identification of the appellant Vlatko Kupreskic which was rejected by the Trial Chamber, and so again, we submit, great care needs to be taken in deciding that this particular identification of Vlatko Kupreskic can be relied upon, whereas the other identification of him, the Trial Chamber felt, could not be. Again, a piece of evidence which, we submit, taken in isolation really does not add up to evidence which could possibly sustain the conviction of Vlatko Kupreskic. Witness T, I mentioned earlier when I opened my submissions by way of example. Witness T dealt with the alleged unloading of weapons in October of 1992. The Defence case was that what may well have been being unloaded was merchandise, bearing in mind that at the basement of Vlatko Kupreskic's house, which is nearby to his warehouse shop, merchandise is stored. So it wasn't an outright denial that no, this couldn't have taken place, but possibly what was seen was misinterpreted by the witness. It is in those circumstances significant that the distance between Witness T and the activity she claimed to have observed was some 50 metres, and that she was unable, in evidence, to describe the type of weapon. It is also significant that the purported observation took place at dusk. Startlingly, there was no cross-examination of Witness T to challenge this point or to test the reliability of the observation. The Prosecution suggests that may have been for tactical reasons. We, with the greatest of respect, reject that. It would, we submit, be counsel's duty if there is a dispute, as there clearly was, because Vlatko Kupreskic in evidence denied that this took place, to put that in cross-examination and to test the accuracy or, conversely, unreliability of the purported observation. Unfortunately, that did not take place but we know, as I said, that Vlatko Kupreskic denied the matter in his evidence in trial, at trial. What does that evidence, we ask, really amount to taken by itself? As I already said earlier on in my submissions, this was six months pre the incident on the 4th -- on the 16th of April of 1993 at a time when tension in the Vitez area was between Croats and Serbs, not Croats and Muslims. We submit it is simply too remote a piece of evidence taken by itself to persuade a Tribunal as to -- beyond reasonable doubt as to guilt. Witness H, the disputed sighting of Vlatko Kupreskic on the morning of the 16th of April. The Trial Chamber significantly, we submit, made no finding as to what Vlatko Kupreskic was actually doing, but speculated, in our contention, really, by saying that the mere presence without evidence of any actual activity such as participation was sufficient, mere presence as proof of guilt or going towards taken with other evidence proof of guilt. I have been told that Witness H is heavily attacked, if I may use that expression, by those who represent both Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic and that they will develop arguments as to the unreliability of Witness H who affects their clients significantly. So I will, if I may, adopt in advance remarks and submissions as to the unreliability of Witness H, but I underline in relation to that witness the fact that the Trial Chamber simply could not glean or deduce what it was said that Vlatko Kupreskic was actually doing at that time. It is possible, possible, given that he indicated in his evidence that there was a point in time when he had to leave the shelter to where he had fled with his wife and children, that he had tried to see what had become of his father and, therefore, came out of the shelter in order to see what was going on and whether he could render assistance to his father. So it is possible that his presence was, in fact, innocent as opposed to guilty, significantly in that regard as I have already said, and I'm sorry to have to repeat myself, significantly in that regard, he is not said to go doing anything specific. I now turn, Chapter 5 to the issue of the police evidence. This evidence seems to have the -- crept up, if I can put it that way, on the Trial Chamber as the trial unfolded. It's important to remember that what it really emanated from was simply two pieces of paper, the exhibit numbers that I have already given. It would be our submission that the importance which the Trial Chamber eventually gave to that police evidence in their judgement may not have been apparent to any of the parties during the course of the trial. That it was, in our submission, in the final analysis, or appears in the final analysis to have been regarded as evidence of importance in the judgement which coloured the way in which Vlatko Kupreskic was perceived by the Trial Chamber. And it's as against that shading of him as somebody who, in some suspicious or murky nebulous way was connected with the police that appears to have, as it were, breathed life into the other aspects of the circumstantial and identification evidence which I've already referred to and effectively, if I can use that phrase, put a guilty gloss on pieces of evidence which might otherwise might have been considered to be relatively innocuous or make weight pieces of evidence. It is why, in our submission, one has to tread with great care with the police evidence and, of course, this is evidence where we submit that the additional evidence we have been allowed to present to the Appeals Chamber has gone a long way to explain and neutralise the effect of that police evidence and, indeed, to support what the appellant at trial was really left on his own to say unsupported. I refer, of course, to the evidence of ADB, ADC, and Miro Lazarevic. It puts that evidence in a new light. We stand by our written submissions. It is of great significance, we submit, that that evidence served as it was, filed as it was, I apologise, on the 5th of September last year was not evidence which was rebutted in any way by counter-evidence called by the Prosecution. And indeed during the course of the presentation of that evidence, Your Honours may remember, that certain matters were put in cross-examination to the witnesses which resulted in our having faxed over from Croatia a monthly or, I'm sorry, a wages logbook, the exhibit reference is AD/14/3/ter which supported what one of the witnesses had been saying as to the way in which the system of payment and the system of logging for work done was calculated. In our submission, that was a real glimpse of the voracity of the evidence which we called as additional evidence to deal with that topic of this appellant's involvement with the police, that he truly was an individual who was working part time to put an inventory together. He was juggling that with his full-time job in the Sutra shop and his business, no training was undertaking. The exotic job descriptions which appeared on some of the documentation could not have been undertaken without training and, indeed, Your Honours will remember that we were able to call evidence which demonstrated the palpable inaccuracy on one of the documents upon which the Trial Chamber placed great reliance. There were several names on that list, Vlatko Kupreskic's included, where there simply was a complete error in relation to the nature of the job that was put down on the piece of paper. We submit that had the Trial Chamber had the benefit of that additional evidence, a doubt would have been cast upon the cogency of those two pieces of paper such that the Trial Chamber would have been in doubt as to being able to act on it. We submit that with that, the picture changes radically; that the murky, nebulous, empty gloss which is put on other pieces of evidence simply falls away. My last chapter is really by way of conclusion. We submit that the effect and impact of the additional evidence is to cast doubt upon, firstly, the correctness of the most important Prosecution witness, L, in particular, M and O. They go to the heart of the case. Take them out of the picture and one is really left with very little. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Further, the additional evidence as to the appellant's involvement with the police confirms the appellant Vlatko Kupreskic's account and neutralises that evidence, and again takes away what the Trial Chamber, by the time of the judgement, seemed to have considered to have been a significant plank in the case against him, taking that away, taking away witnesses that go to the heart of the evidence, L -- to the heart of the case against him, L, M, and O, and one frankly is left with very little. In our submission, the reasonable and obvious question, with what is left, could a reasonable tribunal, left with the remnants of the evidence, be sure of guilt? In our submission, the answer to that must be no, there could or might be a doubt on the evidence that remains. To come back to my spider's web analogy, sufficient of the threads of that spider's web have been broken by the additional evidence that the web, in our submission, disintegrates, and this conviction cannot be sustained. The first finding that the Trial Chamber made in relation to Vlatko Kupreskic is at paragraph 462. The Trial Chamber takes into account the undisputed evidence that, prior to the conflict, this accused was on good terms with Muslims and displayed no nationalist or ethnic prejudice. "The Trial Chamber also takes into account the evidence, again undisputed, that he suffers from a congenital heart condition and as a result was excused from military service." That is an instructive insight into this particular appellant's background. In our submission, in his case, this appeal should be allowed. I hope that in those submissions I have answered the questions that were posed of me, or potential questions that were posed of me before I embarked upon my submissions in relation to the appeal against conviction. Of course, I am willing to assist if there are any others, just before I hand over for the final chapter to my worthy co-counsel, Mr. Livingston, to deal with sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, I think that we'll hear Mr. Livingston, and then if there are any questions on the entire submission of your client, we'll hear those.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, can I start by making an apology to His Honour Judge Pocar who I simply cannot see from where I stand at all. But perhaps it's more important what my words say than what I appear like. Your Honour, this is Chapter 7, sentence, and I'll try and rattle through it. I think I've got about 13 minutes or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Livingston, please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Livingston, will you speak into the microphone. The translators are having some difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Right. Our submission in a nutshell is this: The sentence imposed on Vlatko Kupreskic on Count 1 was one of six years. We say that that was too long. We don't analyse the situation, as do the Prosecution, in terms of looking at each of the arguments set out in the appellant's brief on sentence individually. We say that the proper approach is to look at all those arguments, and that if you look at all those arguments together, take them together, they indicate that if the Trial Chamber had taken them into account and balanced them up properly, the sentence would have been shorter. It is, of course, to be noted at the end of the judgement, it's paragraph 854 of the judgement, that the Trial Chamber set out what factors they took into account. It's 854 to 857. There aren't really very many of them. There's a recital in paragraph 854 of the finding of guilt, there's a very brief summary in the following paragraph of the basis of it, and then it's noted in the following paragraph that he was on good terms with Muslims and displayed no nationalist or ethnic prejudice, and then there's a reference to the fact that he didn't surrender, which is, in a sense, not a point in his favour in the sense that it was found to be mitigation for the other defendants. Let me say straight away that one sympathises with any court which is not assisted by counsel in reaching its conclusions on sentence, and sadly that was the case in this particular case. Your Honour, I think there's no dispute that the starting point for consideration of sentence is Article 24, and in particular, the main factors which you have to look at in Article 24(2) are the gravity of the offence and the individual circumstances of the convicted person. There are other matters, of course, dealt with in Rule 101, but those are perhaps the primary matters. Can I say that in the interests of brevity, I can't deal with every point in the brief. I adopt the brief; I adopt what my learned friend Mr. Clegg said in morning in relation to raising matters which weren't raised before the Trial Chamber. Your Honour, having dealt with the contents of Article 24, one comes to the point that is raised in paragraph 5 of the appellant's brief on sentence, which is that the Chamber should have regard to the need to develop a principled sentencing scale or gradation which reflects such factors as (a) the place or level of the defendant in the scheme of things for which he falls to be sentenced; and (b) his actual involvement in the crimes committed. That's something which the Prosecution take issue with. They deal with it, as I understand it, at paragraph 38.11 of their respondent's brief, and they say, "no hierarchy of relative criminal culpability," and then they purport to explain why. Well, I have to say the weight of authority from this Tribunal is against them on that. The two main cases dealing with this gradation point are the Tadic Appeals Chamber decision and the Appeals Chamber decision in Aleksovski. In the Tadic appeal decision, the matter is dealt with at paragraph 51. And again I mention that particularly because it appears from the Prosecutor's footnote that the reference that they're referring to as "Tadic Sentencing Judgement, para 70," that doesn't seem to be the right reference. It's some paragraphs 51 to 58. But looking at paragraph 51, the submissions made by the appellant in that case about the need to develop a recognisable sentencing tariff or range of sentences are set out, and at paragraph 55, these words occur: "In the opinion of the Appeals Chamber, the Trial Chamber's decision, when considered against the background of the jurisprudence of the International Tribunal and of the Rwandan Tribunal, fails to adequately consider the need for sentences to reflect the relative significance of the role of the appellant in the broader context of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia." And they go on in paragraph 56 to refer to the heinous nature of the defendant's crimes, but pointing out that his level in the command structure, compared to that of his superiors, was low. And the matter is also dealt with in paragraph 184 of the judgement of the Chamber in the Aleksovski case where it's specifically said, "The Trial Chamber was right to emphasise the need to establish a gradation of sentencing," and they refer to the Tadic decision which has been made before. So in my submission, the appellant is on strong ground when he says that that is the path which the -- this Chamber should follow in dealing with sentence in this case. In other words, try and place this appellant in his proper place in the scale of things in the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. They also say in the same paragraph, Prosecution 38.11, "It may be expected that the conduct of aiding and abetting will normally be regarded as less grave than the conduct of actually committing the crime, but this will not necessarily always be the case." It's very hard to see how that proposition stands up at all and they go on to say as a purported example, "A person who is convicted of ordering the commission of a war crime is equally guilty with the person actually committing it," but the whole point of that, surely, that the person convicted of ordering it is a principal, and convicted as a principal or as a co-perpetrator or whatever word you want to use, and not as an aider and abettor. So in my submission, that argument doesn't assist the Prosecution at all, and the proposition which the appellant puts forward and that the conduct of an aider and abettor will always be less serious than that of a principal stands, and should be applied in this particular case. Paragraph 38.14 of the Prosecution's submissions say that, "determination of the sentence," submits that, "The determination of what sentence would be commensurate with inherent gravity of the accused conduct should not be made by comparison with the alleged acts of others known or unknown to the Trial Chamber." Well, again, I submit that that is quite at odds with the approach of this Chamber in both Tadic and Aleksovski, and it's very difficult to see how you can form any sort of gradation of sentencing without having regard to this appellant's conduct, and comparing it with the alleged acts of others known and unknown to the Trial Chamber. So in my submission, when one looks at the point that's made in the following paragraph by the Prosecution relying on the Celebici appeal, it's very it difficult to see that how that has any application to this either because they quote this passage, they say that: "A gradation based on the accused's level in the overall hierarchy in the conflict, and then a quote from the case, '... does not entail a low sentence for all those in low level of the overall command structure. On the contrary a sentence must always reflect the inherent gravity of the crime which requires consideration of the particular circumstances of the cases as well as the form and degree of the participation of the accused in the crime.'" Well, with respect to the Prosecution, the appellant, the appellant is submitting exactly what the Appeals Chamber in Celebici said. He's not saying what the Prosecution seem to think that he's saying. This appellant -- it's never said been said that this appellant was in a low level of -- in the command structure. He never had any command position at all. What is being said is that in looking at his position in the round, he is a low-level defendant with a very low level compared to others of responsibility for, in this case, what happened in Ahmici. He's an aider and abettor, and his role in aiding and abetting whilst, of course, serious, mustn't be elevated to a level which it doesn't warrant. But what we are saying is you ought to look at the gravity of the offence, and if you do that, looking at his level of responsibility, he is a low-level defendant who should be sentenced as such. The Prosecution then go on to deal with the issue of sentences in other cases, that's paragraph 38.18. I'm rapidly running out of time. I'm being told I've got three minutes left. Let me simply say that I rely on the cases which are set out in the appellant's brief on that. In my submission, it is strongly arguable that you if you look at the facts even in this case for Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, Zoran has, of course, been sentenced on the basis of a low-level command, but they are both sentenced, paragraph 852 of the judgement,"... as principals guilty of persecution for the expulsion of Muslim civilians, individuals including children, from Ahmici, Santici, and its environs, destruction of Bosnian Muslim homes and property, and their active presence in the area whilst armed." What we say is if even eight years is a proper sentence for Mirjan Kupreskic, there is not an adequate reflection of the lesser responsibility of Vlatko Kupreskic in all the circumstances. I haven't said anything about the other point about the minimum sentence, however, I think that's probably adequately dealt with in the written briefs. I don't think I can add very greatly to that. Mr. Pavkovic has dealt partly with the SFRY law. I rely on Article 154 in the old SFRY sentencing law about persecution, and I do say that the fact that the essence that that is racial persecution is very relevant to this case, because persecution in this Tribunal is equally fundamentally based on racial discrimination. That's the reason why the acts have been committed. So in my submission, one shouldn't ignore that as a factor. Well, I think I'm now probably about 30 seconds over time. Unless there are any other particular matters which Your Honour and any of your colleagues wish me to deal with, those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Livingston. Let me see if my colleagues have questions for either Mr. Abell or Mr. Livingston. Mr. Abell, I'm sorry, I have two questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I shall endeavour to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I want to make sure that I understand. When you talk about the evidence before the Trial Chamber, that the Trial Chamber actually heard, not the 115 evidence that we did, you refer to it several times as tenuous. Are you -- and you relied quite strongly on the light in which that evidence should newly be perceived in view of the evidence that came in under 115. But are you making a separate argument that the evidence that was before the Trial Chamber was insufficient to permit a conviction of guilty for those crimes for which he was held responsible regardless of the 115? The reason I ask this, and then you can answer it in one, is it that Mr. Clegg's answer, and I think you've adopted his general interpretation of the way 115 should be interpreted, if, indeed, 115 evidence meets the standard of the "could" or "might," then, according to Mr. Clegg, in most cases, the fall in the middle, that don't fall clearly credible or clearly incredible, you need to remit to the Trial Chamber. Is that something that you want for your client who is at the same time asking to have a minimum sentence fit, or how do you bring those two together?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: There are two issues, in our submission, encapsulated in Your Honour's question. The first issue is this: How do we put the tenuous aspects, as I've referred to it? Ground A of our grounds of appeal, and I didn't want to spend time elaborating it too much in my oral submissions, but we do, in the alternative to relying on the Rule 115 evidence adduced, we do, in the alternative, say that based on the evidence available before the Trial Chamber, there was not enough evidence for the Trial Chamber safely to conclude beyond reasonable doubt that this man was guilty even as an aider and abettor of persecution. So it is an alternative ground of appeal, ground A in our grounds of appeal. The second -- I hope that deals with the -- as it were, Your Honour's primary question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes, I know that you had said that in your brief. I just wanted to make sure that that was still your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes, and as I say, we rely on our pleadings and really the oral argument is complimentary to it. But can I deal with the second issue which is this: Going back in time, at the time that we filed our Rule 115 application, in the discussion on the law in that Rule 115 application, and I may need a little time to hunt out the precise paragraph - I'm sure I will be able to furnish it for Your Honour tomorrow if not later this afternoon - we do deal with the issue as to what should happen and we did, at that stage, suggest that it may be that if Rule 115 evidence is admitted, that at that stage, the matter should be remitted to the Trial Chamber. But in fact, the course that was taken by the Appeals Chamber was to move straight to the -- was for the Appeals Chamber to hear the additional evidence and move straight to the appeal. So we would submit that there were two routes that could have been taken arguably. One was to remit to the Trial Chamber once the Rule 115 additional evidence was admitted and let the Trial Chamber, as it were, grapple with the evidentiary issues. The other route is the route that has been taken which is that the Appeals Chamber listens to the additional evidence and then is left with the position that we are now in, and I adopt what my learned friend Mr. Clegg was saying, which is this: that when you haven't heard the evidence available to the Trial Chamber, you haven't seen the demeanour of the witnesses, you can't really make an assessments or an evaluation of that. You are back to the question, in our submission, Your Honours are back to the question of simply this: Might or could a reasonable Trial Chamber with this additional evidence have had a doubt? That's what it comes to. Might they have reached a different verdict?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But Mr. Abell, you're asking us to make that decision; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That is the ultimate decision. And may I actually cite an authority? Will Your Honours bear with me. This, in fact, is a very recent -- I'm sorry, it's not that recent, it's about a year old. It's the case of Michael Davis, Rafael Rowe, and Randolf Johnston. It is a somewhat celebrated case in the United Kingdom. A copy will be handed up to Your Honours. It's on point for the particular question that you ask. This, in fact, is reported at 2001, 1 Criminal Appeal Reports at page 115. The photocopy doesn't reveal the page number. Can I just cite this particular passage. It's paragraph 95: "In our view, the case against all three appellants was formidable. The evidence against Rowe on the counts he faced was overwhelming. However, we are bound to follow the approach set out earlier in this judgement; namely, assuming the irregularities which we have identified had not occurred, would a reasonable jury have been bound to return verdicts of guilty? In all conscience, we cannot say that it would. At this distance, we simply cannot assess the impact which the undisclosed material might have had on the case for and against Johnson." In that case, it was the failure by the Prosecution to disclose material which they had to the Defence. That was absent at the trial. The analogy, of course, here is the additional evidence that you had the -- Your Honours have had the benefit of hearing but, of course, the Trial Chamber didn't. And it's that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I think you've --

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: -- that blunt question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: -- very amply answered my question, Mr. Abell.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'll make sure that a copy of this authority is put before Your Honours.

utterances.text: Thank you. We will now move on to Mr. Radovic. Now, I understand that you and the counsel for Mirjan have decided that you will split the amount of time which is allocated to each of you, not necessarily in half but according to whatever you have worked out.
