utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my previous remarks, I started setting out my objections to the judgement, and I would like to proceed along those lines. I already said that the disposition should be followed, so I don't want to go back to all of that; however, I should like to go back to the judgement itself and to the trial. I think that the judgement does not meet all the standards required of writing a judgement, because I think that it has to be in line with the transcript or, rather, that portion that is being quoted. Because we cannot say that, on the basis of the quoted part of the transcript, one comes to a certain conclusion, and then if you actually look at the transcript, there is a completely different kind of inference that can be made. In addition to everything else, one of the basic ways of conducting proceedings is that this can be done only on the basis of evidence that was presented during proceedings. So if the Court says -- if the Court says, "Right, we have established this or that," or "we have not established this or that," this has to be corroborated by facts, by evidence that was presented during the proceedings; not to come to certain conclusions on the basis of whatever during the proceedings. I shall go back to this a bit later. Then, furthermore, the Court did not act according to Article 21 of the Statute; namely, did not uphold the fact that all persons should be equal before the Court. The best proof of this is footnote 589. In this footnote, 589, which is part of the judgement and which was written in a way which we find incredible, it says that Defence witnesses are not believed or, rather, a certain fact is not established only because it was established by the Defence witnesses; although the Prosecutor did not challenge this in any way and present any counter-evidence. If we were to proceed along those lines, if we look at the judgement itself, then everything that the Defence has proven during proceedings, especially with respect to Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic, was pointless, because whatever we did or did not do, the Court did not believe us because, according to this footnote, the Defence witnesses are simply not believed. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber does not uphold that principle in terms of 162, paragraph 162, of the judgement. What we said was that the conflict, on the 20th of October, 1992, was provoked by the Muslims; however, the Trial Chamber bore in mind their final conclusion, and their final conclusion was that in Ahmici, there was not a unit of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and in order to avoid a conclusion that is contrary to the set objectives, so to speak, the Trial Chamber concludes, in Article 162, the following, I quote: "Some local Muslims and Croats either took part in the conflict or assisted those who were fighting." Before that, it was also ascertained in 162 that this conflict was provoked by the Muslims. So this conclusion by the Trial Chamber, both in respect of the Croats and in respect of the Muslims, is in direct contravention to the evidence produced; namely, in relation to the Croats, not a single Prosecution witness said that the Croats from Ahmici took part in the conflict, except that one or two witnesses claimed that only in respect of Dragan Papic. No one else. And Dragan Papic has been acquitted. As for who the Muslims were, the members of the BH army who took part in the conflict of the 20th of October, we are relying only on Prosecution witnesses so that we would not bring ourselves into the position of relying upon our own witnesses, because the Trial Chamber did not believe Defence witnesses. For example, witness Abdulah Ahmic, then Witness B, Mehmed Ahmic, Fahrudin Ahmic, Witness N, Witness V, Witness AA, and many other witnesses who spoke about this subject said that members of the BH army who caused the conflict on the 20th of October, 1992 were exclusively inhabitants of the Muslim part of Ahmici, who were assisted by villagers from the neighbouring village of Vrhovine. In addition to that, the Trial Chamber claims in 125 and 511, these two respective paragraphs of the judgement, that the Defence produced evidence on crimes that were committed by the Muslims against the Croats before the 16th of April, 1993 with a view to justifying the crime that was committed against the Muslims in Ahmici. Not at a single point did the Defence counsel either for Zoran or Mirjan Kupreskic produce evidence for the reasons that are mentioned in the disposition of the judgement. When the Presiding Judge actually asked us why we are producing this evidence, we explained the reasons why we were doing that, and now I'm going to repeat these reasons. The reason for producing evidence concerning Muslim crimes against the Croats were the following: to justify the state of mind of the accused at the moment when they received information that they were supposed to evacuate their families, because there was information that, on the 16th of April, 1993, the Muslims would attack the Croats. The Kupreskics were at such a low level, or, rather, they were not part of the military or civilian authorities at all; therefore, they could not have accurate information; therefore, they got information from Croat sources and they took that information as correct. If this information had been correct -- or, rather, they thought this information was correct in view of what they knew concerning previous incidents, and that was the only reason why we produced this evidence. There's another interesting detail showing different approaches to evidence with regard to Prosecution Exhibit P353. In paragraphs 342 and 377 of the judgement, it is claimed that this is a document that contains a list of the reservists of the military component of the HVO. In paragraphs 421 and 773 of the judgement respectively, on the basis of this same document, it is established that the accused was an active member of the HVO. What is an active and what is a passive or, rather, what is a reserve member of the army? I am going to refer to that when I go back to the facts. This is a simple fact, and during the trial itself, we had long debates on this. At one point, we were already talking about active reservists and reserve activists, and obviously the two are contradictory and these two notions cannot be brought together in any way. In addition to that, in paragraph 423 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber did not carry out its duty in terms of establishing the exact state of affairs in order to be able to establish beyond any reasonable doubt certain relevant facts. In paragraph 423, it is stipulated that both accused persons, perhaps on the 15th of April, were at work, and perhaps in the evening, they were the guests at the house of Ivica Kupreskic. On that day, in the early evening hours, Ivica Kupreskic's wife had arrived from Germany, where she had enjoyed the status of a refugee. The Trial Chamber had to make its views quite clear, whether they were at work or whether they were at Ivica Kupreskic's. Perhaps they were; perhaps they weren't. And this is not the way a judgement should read. However, what is particularly interesting is how it is being expounded that already on the 15th of April, the accused knew what would happen on the 16th of April. In paragraph 423 of the judgement, it is said that they had to know about that, and then in paragraph 773 of the judgement, it is not said that they had to know about it, but it was said that they simply knew about it. I already said that during that these proceedings, the same facts are evaluated in different ways in the case of different accused persons. So I would like to refer to statements made by protected Witness AT. I'm not going to refer to the substance of this person's statement at great length, I'm just going to talk about the possibility of using this statement; that is, the possibility that we had, the Defence counsel for Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic. And I don't know whether we have to move into private session in order to be able to speak about that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic, I'm somewhat guided by your own appraisal of what you're about to say. I think we probably should err on the side of caution if you think that it's likely to get into anything identifying or closed material. If you think it's not, I'll go along with your judgement at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think that in this part there is no need for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. You'll be careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is one thing I learned, and that is that I am always guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I said "careful," not "guilty," Mr. Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When using the statement of Witness AT, different standards were applied in the case of different accused, and also the Defence counsel for Vlatko Kupreskic could not use that part of the transcript. However, we proceed from the decision made by the Trial Chamber on May 29th, and that is when Vlatko Kupreskic expressed their belief that the transcript could be used by both parties. We believe that on the basis of this ruling of the Chamber, we can also use the these statements and -- or rather these parts of the transcript so we are going to use them. And I believe that this ruling by the Appeals Chamber that others can also use these statements is in line with beneficium cohesiones which implies that if one the accused can draw on something, then the other accused also have the right to do that. If this interpretation of ours were not to be accepted then, again, there would be an absurd situation. Actually, with the assistance of the statement of the mentioned witness, the credibility of the witnesses who speak about the presence of soldiers in the vicinity of the Kupreskic house, and then without the statement of AT, these statements would be believed. But in relation to the third Kupreskic, it would not be believed. There can only be one truth. There cannot be one truth for -- in one case that the soldiers were there, or another truth, in other case, that the soldier were not there. In addition to that, in the judgement, different witnesses are approached in a different manner. For example, the Trial Chamber did not believe Witness C because at the given time, this person was young and under stress. This is a person who identified a person whom he or she saw during the day. For the same reason, Witness G is not believed either. Witness KL, who was relevant to ten counts of the indictment, is not believed. It is not that the witness is not believed, but the Trial Chamber says that he was confused in terms of the identification although he saw these persons whom he identified under electric light. On the other hand, the Chamber believes Witness H who identified persons in her house where the lights were not on irrespective of the many objections that were raised with regard to the authenticity and the truthfulness of her statement. The Trial Chamber does not refer to most of the objections made in respect of her testimony, but only some. Also, the Trial Chamber is claiming something that does not correspond to the case itself. In 163, it is claimed that the Muslims left the village and that the Croats did not. However, Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, through their own testimonies and also through Defence witnesses, sought to prove and proved that they, together with their families, left Ahmici and returned to their houses only when the Muslims returned. Actually, they believed that they were safe in their village only if, in that same village, their Muslim neighbours felt safe as well. Without the safety of one, there could be no safety of the other. With respect of Witness H, I have to say something that the Prosecutor is not going to like, and that is that we have reason to suspect that the Prosecutor has not met his obligation stemming from Rule 68 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, namely: There has been no exculpatory evidence presented. I would like to state the following: In the system of criminal procedure in the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, there were several authorities that would question a witness. According to that system, it was not the investigators of the Prosecution and of the Defence who would question witnesses. Witness would be questioned by policemen. In the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it would be the office for the establishment of war crimes and also an investigating judge. That it was so is shown by the fact of -- that Dijana Ajanovic, a senior investigating judge from Zenica testified to that effect. The first statement that we had from Witness H is the one that she made before an investigating judge of the higher court in Zenica, and that was in the month of December 1993, that is to say, about eight months after events that she testified about. As opposed to her, her mother, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Witness SA, and her aunt, Witness EE, and her grandfather, Witness KL, we have records of police investigations that are dated immediately after these refugees came to Zenica. When they were first questioned by the police in Zenica, neither KL or SA did not identify the perpetrators. So they explained why they did not or, rather, they explained that the attackers wore caps over their heads with slits for the eyes, and the nose, and the mouth. Because of these caps, they could not identify anyone. What is particularly interesting is that in separate interviews, both KL and SA gave identical descriptions of the attackers in view of how they had been masked. As for these first interviews, there is no such record for Witness H. With regard to the two mentioned witnesses, there are also statements that they made before the state office for the establishment of war crimes of Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, the Muslim part. However, as for Witness H, there is no such statement either. Witness KL mentions Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic for the first time during the interview with the investigating judge in Zenica in October 1993. However, at that time, the witness does not say that he recognised them. He says that there were two soldiers who looked like Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic the most. So he is mentioning them on the basis of similarity, not in terms of identifying them with certainty. Now, something really interesting happens. In the judgement in which the Trial Chamber acquits Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic with regard to the events that took place in Witness KL's house, the Trial Chamber says that KL is a truthful witness. However, because of conversations with others, this witness convinced himself that these soldiers were Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic and that, therefore, he mentioned that these were soldiers who looked like them. In addition, the Trial Chamber mentions that KL managed to convince himself on the basis of conversations with his granddaughter, Witness H. Despite the fact that until his statement given to the -- that apart from his statement given to the investigating judge, we do not have any statement that would be given by her. Witness Dijana Ajanovic confirmed that the villagers of Ahmici talked to each other about what they had been through, and that they made certain conjectures as to who the attackers could be. When the Trial Chamber states that Witness KL acted under the influence of his granddaughter then, with all due respect to the Court, I have to say that the Trial Chamber is not familiar with the customs prevalent in Bosnia. Because in Bosnia, it is not a custom for a man, a middle-aged man to listen to what his granddaughter, aged 13, is saying to him. One could only envisage a situation that would be a complete reverse of that one. After Witness KL mentioned this resemblance, in December we have statements given to the investigating judge where both H and her mother, SA, identify the perpetrators with certainty. Furthermore, as regards Witness SA, we believe that the Trial Chamber infringed on the right of the accused or of his Defence. I will try to be brief when presenting this argument. Witness SA was on the list made up by the Prosecution, one of the witnesses that were to have been heard. But the Prosecutor was also able to see the various statements that she had given, and the Prosecutor has given up on presenting her testimony although they had led us to believe, up until the very last moment, that she would be presented as a witness before the Court. However, this was not the fact because her daughter, Witness H, states that her mother did not arrive in The Hague to testify, but as her escort, to accompany her. The Prosecutor explained that the reason why they had given up on her testimony was because Witness SA was ill, and then what happened next is something that I had not experienced in my entire professional career and I believe that it is also your case. The social worker testified as to the health of the witness and not a doctor. I'm not -- just a moment, please allow me to finish. I am not really familiar with the Anglo-Saxon common law system but I am sure that it is impossible for a social worker to present medical evidence. My colleague from the Prosecution would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Yapa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the facts, we also believe that it has not been correctly established, as regards the events in Ahmici on the 20th of October, the participation of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic in the HVO before the 18th of April; the command responsibility of Zoran Kupreskic in April 1993; the participation of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I apologise. This is too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic, I think you have to go a little bit slower. That's the translator's request.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Let me repeat, then. The facts have not been established fully or correctly as regards the events in Ahmici on the 20th of October, 1992; the existence of the BH army in Ahmici - this would be item B, and I will refer to that in the end if we have some time to spare, because this part is not so important for our defence; the participation of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic in the HVO before the 18th of April, 1993; the command role played by Zoran Kupreskic; the participation of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic in the events of the 16th of April, 1993; and who it was that planned and carried out the attack on Ahmici. So let me begin with the events in Ahmici on the 20th of October, 1992. Paragraph 162 of the judgement indicates that the Trial Chamber has correctly stated that the Muslims caused the conflict on that date, and the Trial Chamber established that members of the BH army took part in this conflict, as did members of the HVO, which were not from Ahmici. In these proceedings, a lot has been said about the HVO without properly defining this entity. Just to make things clear, the HVO was a civil authority and, at the same time, it had a military component. So when you talk about the HVO, you have to specify whether you're referring to the civilian authority or to the military component of the overall HVO government. The facts have been incompletely established in as much as it has not been stated where the BH army members who took part in the conflict came from, and the facts have been wrongly established because it is stated that only some local Muslims and some local Croats took part in the conflict. The lack of precision in the judgement itself is caused by the necessity to explain the events, to provide an explanation for the events of the 16th of April, where it is stated that there were no BH army units in Ahmici. Because if the conflict of the 20th of October was caused by a BH army unit from Ahmici and if it participated in the conflict, then it would not be possible for this unit from Ahmici to just disappear and for it not to be there on the 16th of April, 1993. In the wartime circumstances that were prevalent in Bosnia at that time, a military unit could only increase in strength. It was impossible for it to disappear. To prove my point, I draw your attention to the way in which the BH army was organised, and the expert witness Asim Dzambasovic, a Prosecution expert witness, testified to that effect. In his expert testimony, which was very fair and correct - and we did not have any objections to his testimony - he explained that the BH army at the time was organised on the territorial principle, which means that all members from a single locality or village were, at the same time, members of a certain BH army unit. The Prosecution witnesses' testimony indicate that the BH army members were, indeed, from Ahmici. I need not refer to Defence witnesses because we have ample evidence provided by the Prosecution witnesses. They confirmed that they had set up and defended the roadblock on the basis of an order they received from their superior command. I will not now go into details of the witness statements. I will just mention the names of witnesses: Abdulah Ahmic, this witness has been identified in public; Witness B; Witness Fahrudin Ahmic; Witness N; Witness V; Witness AA. And it is stated incorrectly in this particular paragraph of the judgement that some Croats from Ahmici participated on an individual basis in all this, because the only Croat mentioned by Prosecution witnesses is Dragan Papic. It is also incorrect that only Muslims had fled Ahmici, because Zoran and Mirjan also did, and I have already spoken about that. This would conclude my presentation as regards the 20th of October. I will now say a few things about whether Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic were in the HVO before the 16th of April, 1993 or, to be more specific, the 18th of April, when they claimed that they had been mobilised. Paragraph 377 of the judgement refers to the claims of the Prosecution that Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic were, in fact, in the HVO on the basis of the fact that they had both done their national service and that they were both on the list of the Vitez Brigade, registered at the Vitez Brigade, in the period from April 1992 to January 1996. In particular for Zoran Kupreskic, it is stated that Witness JJ indicates that he was a member of the HVO - this is paragraph 378 of the judgement - and it is also alleged that he was some kind of a commander. The claim that he was a commander is allegedly based on the statements by Witness B and by the witness Abdulah Ahmic. That's paragraph 379. Paragraph 421 of the judgement, in this paragraph, the Trial Chamber states that they had been convinced, that they're satisfied that both accused were active members of the HVO, referring to Prosecution Exhibit P353 as regards Zoran Kupreskic. In paragraph 442 it is stated that Zoran Kupreskic was a local HVO commander and that his activities were not limited to assigning guards or guard duties, referring to Witnesses JJ, B, and Abdulah Ahmic, and the crucial piece of evidence in this respect is that he was a reserve officer of the former JNA and that he was in a position of management in his company where he worked and, therefore, he was used to the exercise of authority. First of all, Exhibit P353 does not prove that Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic were active members of the HVO prior to their mobilisation. As regards Mirjan Kupreskic, he never signed this document which means that he did not agree with the time period stipulated in that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic, I'm sorry to interrupt you again but I am reminded that the translators absolutely have to have a break under their rules, and so I think we will have a short break now which will go to 4.30 and --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was really getting into my stride.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but they do have their rules and we will -- you'll have at least another sizeable period to hit your stride as soon as we get back at 4.30, okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic, apologies again for the interruption, but it was necessary, and we will now go until approximately 5.15 and hope you can get back in stride. The remainder of the time that you and Ms. Glumac have will be saved for tomorrow morning. Will she be taking over in the morning or will you be continuing in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She will be taking over tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll let you get right back in stride now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit P353 is evidence that the accused were not members of the HVO because, according to that document, they were mobilised between the 16th and 28th of April. With regard to documents containing other information which is the opposite of that, then we should believe the document that was issued at the relevant time and not one that was issued later and one which witnesses, for example, DA testified was issued because shares were being handed out, and the same was testified by Witness II and this refers to Dragan Papic as is visible from paragraph 355. In the judgement, it is stated that Zoran Kupreskic was a military commander based on the testimonies of Abdulah Ahmic, B, and JJ -- BY and JJ. And they say that after the outbreak of the conflict, this was so, but they do not say anything about the time of the 16th of April and the time immediately preceding this. So it is completely irrelevant was Zoran Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Kupreskic was doing before the 20th of October. Witness Y said that Zoran Kupreskic had told him that he would stop assigning guard duties and Zoran Kupreskic, himself, according to Witness JJ, said he wanted to get rid of this duty and that he did so follows from the testimony of Zoran Kupreskic and the statement of Dragan Vidovic who took over this task in the village and who became the person who assigned guard duties in the village. Therefore, on the 16th of April, there is no evidence to show that Zoran Kupreskic was a commander at that time. I wish to draw attention to the statement of JJ who said that commanders were selected according to their political suitability. And according to D21/1, it follows that an intelligence officer drew up a report on Zoran Kupreskic saying that he was not in favour of the policy of the HDZ before the war, in favour of establishing a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a Croatian national entity, ethnic entity. Witness JJ was a person who did not know anything from her own observation but only from hearsay evidence from Zoran Kupreskic, and we shall say more about this later on, about this witness. Zoran Kupreskic is not listed among the commanders at any rank among the eight documents which have been admitted as fresh evidence in the appeals procedure. He had nothing to do with ordering and carrying out the attack. I would now like to ask to pass into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, please check the distances as well and see who is telling the truth and who is trying to misrepresent the facts. So we have now taken care of ADA, and now we're moving on to the most sensitive issue at all, and that is something that we already mentioned: Are the two of them individuals who took part in the attack on Ahmici? As for Witness SA, I have already said the most important things that were to be said. Now we move on to Witness H, who's supposed to be a protective witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I shall first deal with the first part which is not protected, and then I'll move on to the rest which is protected. She is the only witness who confirmed that both of the Kupreskics were in her house at the time of these events, and these events consisted of the following: that a Muslim was killed in front of that house; in front of that house, her father was killed as well; her house was torched; and she together with her mother and her two sisters was expelled. However, now something very strange happens. The Trial Chamber itself is convinced that this is hardly acceptable, so they start with the ruling of the appeals court in England, quoting it and saying that that judgement says that as far as ascertaining the identity of a perpetrator is concerned, the court had to act very cautiously because there is a danger involved in such testimonies; that is, that a witness can easily make a mistake in terms of identification; and that even a truthful witness who made a mistake may seem very convincing at first sight. That is 339(C) of this judgement. Now, why does the Trial Chamber believe Witness H? The only reason they give for this is that they find her testimony convincing. The Court cannot act in this way. The Court has to say why they find a certain witness truthful. Even when there is an eyewitness, a single eyewitness, there are also auxiliary facts, so to speak, which can prove or disprove that the witness is saying the truth. We had hard evidence when we tried to check Witness H's testimony, and our evidence proved that she was not telling the truth. The best proof of this is the statement that she made before an investigating judge. Before an investigating judge, she made a statement and she mentioned numerous circumstances and facts that are contradictory to what she said during the trial here. When confronted with the statement that she made to the investigating judge, then at the very end she ascertained that she did not give any statement to an investigating judge in Zenica. She even repeated that assertion when the Prosecutor said to her, "How can you claim that you never made a statement to the investigating judge in Zenica when yesterday, when we were preparing you for testimony before this Trial Chamber, I showed you this statement?" Then she remembered that the Prosecutor showed her that statement, but she nevertheless adhered to her previous statement that she did not give any statement to the investigating judge in Zenica. In order to show that this witness was not telling the truth, we called as a witness the investigating judge - the Trial Chamber accepted this - and the witness judge confirmed before the Trial Chamber that this person did make a statement before her and that she wrote down everything this person said. The witness, Witness H, made a statement in Zenica, therefore, which is quite different from the testimony she gave in this courtroom. We dealt with this in detail in our brief, my colleague Ms. Slokovic-Glumac and I, so I don't want to go into that again. My colleague will, though. The main point of this is that whenever we wanted to check what she was saying, it turned out she was not telling the truth. We can find further evidence that she was not telling the truth that namely, in her claim, that she knows the Kupreskic brothers well. However, when she was supposed to speak about that, actually how well she knew them, then she said that Zoran Kupreskic worked in the shop of Ivica Kupreskic, and in the proceedings it was ascertained that Zoran Kupreskic never worked in any kind of shop. That he was head of some kind of a maintenance plant in the explosives factory in Vitez, and it was Mirjan Kupreskic who worked in Ivica Kupreskic's shop. Not only that, for a while, before the 16th of April, Mirjan Kupreskic did not work in that shop at all. He went to work in Ivica Kupreskic's shop in Vitez whereas in this other shop there was another man who was employed. Then also, she said that she recognised Zoran Kupreskic by his height. I'm asking you, Your Honours, who can recognise anyone by his or her height? By one's height, one can recognise only persons who were extremely tall and therefore stand out, or if somebody is a dwarf. However, if somebody is of average height, you cannot really identify anyone by height. Then also she said that she identified Zoran Kupreskic because of his receding hairline. You have his photographs from that period. You also have his pictures from that period when he was engaged in folk dancing. Now in prison he started getting bald a bit, but not at that time. Then also she said she identified him by his voice, 80 per cent by his voice as he was shouting. However, when she was asked whether she had ever heard him shout in her life, she said "No." So now I'm asking you the following: How can you identify someone by his shouting voice if you had never heard that shouting voice before? Also, she said that the persons or, rather, the soldiers who were in her house had, on their backs, some kind of barrels. These barrels were actually a Russian made weapon called zoljas, some kind of rocket launchers that were used in the JNA and then later on by the various armies that were waging war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, that is a sophisticated weapon, and not all the soldiers had that. Who are the soldiers who had that? We can see is that from Witness AT's statement. And also his statement is indirectly confirmed by Asim Dzambasovic, a Prosecution witness, and AT is also a Prosecution witness, for that matter. Actually, AT's statement clearly shows what kind of weapons people at the Viteska Brigade had. There were mortars there which is some kind of an artillery weapon depending on its calibre. However, rocket launchers were not involved. Hand-held rocket launchers were only in the hands of the special units including the military police. That this is so is proved by what Asim Dzambasovic said. He explained what zoljas were, and he also confirmed that members of the military police were persons who had specially good weapons, who were very well-trained and who, as a rule, were engaged in attack combat, who would take certain lines. Then they would withdraw and then the locals, as he called them, would come and hold that line that had originally been taken by the special units. So the person who identified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic, I just want to remind you, you've got about five minutes more. I think we're all pretty well --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now the very last thing and the most important thing, but thank you for having said this. It's a good thing you told me, because I almost omitted this. The main objection to Witness H's statement is the question related to visibility in the house itself. In our briefs, we mentioned the witnesses who claimed, for the same period of time, that it was dark. That it was dark is also derived from the statement made by her grandfather, KL. I -- yes, I take this into account. We were also discussing in detail whether there were two lights on in his house, one light on in his house, whether everything that he had said he had seen could be seen, or could not be seen, et cetera. Also in addition to that, in Muslim villages, one knows full well when daybreak comes. That is known because witnesses know when they are called to morning prayer, and that morning prayer has to do with daybreak, dawn. Therefore, it is no secret when daybreak is, and Witness AD showed this the best. The only witness -- the only thing that he could have said was that he did not see what time it was because there was light, but because there was a blaze of fire coming from the house next door. So that is also an objection that we had in terms of this other witness and in terms of visibility. Time is running very short for me now, and my colleague will deal with other matters. As for Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, it has been established that they were not infected by nationalism or ethnic hatred. All their neighbours speak the best of them and Witness S actually says that he trusted Zoran Kupreskic so much that even if he had seen him on the 16th of April when Muslims were being shot at, that he would have approached him, greeted him, and asked him what was going on. We have shown photographs from their folk dancing, et cetera, and we showed what kind of people they were. However, their engagement in the folk dance society is important because it was a multiethnic society, and it was the only society that functioned until the 16th of April. Until then Zoran Kupreskic actually resisted the pressure that was being brought against him to have this society disbanded and to establish a monoethnic society or, rather, he was asked to join the Croatian society that had already been established. Also when the war had already been broken out, JJ's statement shows that he helped Muslims, not only her, but she also asked around and found out that he had helped others as well. Also, Witness JJ's statement clearly shows that he immediately condemned the crime that was committed in Ahmici. So, Your Honours, these are not mitigating circumstances that we are presenting to you now after the judgement has been passed. These are mitigating circumstances that are based on the case material itself, what we proved during the trial itself. If the Prosecutor did not accuse us, in terms of what Witness H said, then we would have presented mitigating circumstances anyway in addition to all of that? Your Honours, please don't mind my saying so, one always has to be very cautious, Mirjan Kupreskic's mother is ill and that was taken as a mitigating circumstance for Mirjan, but it was not taken as a mitigating circumstance for Zoran. But if it is a -- and the one and the same mother. So if it is a mitigating circumstance for one of them, then it should be a mitigating circumstance for the other two. I thank you kindly, and I hope that I remained within the given time frame and I can now give the floor to my learned friend. I thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radovic. We very much appreciate that you stayed within the framework and we're glad you hit your stride. Before we leave, I want to make sure that none of my colleagues have questions, otherwise we'll hear Ms. Glumac tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you very much. We are adjourned for the day.
